slides.title: Change one number in the URL, read someone else's invoice
slides.tldr: Checking that the user is logged in is not enough: before returning anything, check that it belongs to this user. Otherwise you have an IDOR.

blocks.body: Ryan's billing app shows nothing without a login, so he feels safe. One day Kevin opens his own invoice and notices the address is `/api/invoices/1042`. Out of curiosity he types `1043` at the end, and another company's invoice, address and amounts all appear. Kevin cracked no password. The app simply forgot to ask **whose invoice it is**.

marks.tip: This only proves the person is logged in. It does not check whether the invoice is theirs.
Symfony loads whatever invoice `{id}` points to. 1043 or 9999, it makes no difference to it.

blocks.caption: Kevin only changed the id, and nobody asked who owns the invoice

actors.tip: A legitimate user, logged in with his own password. His own invoice is 1042.

actors.label: API
actors.tip: The Symfony controller. It only checks that the request carries a valid login.

actors.label: Database
actors.tip: Every company's invoices sit in one table. It returns whichever id is asked for.

messages.tip: He just added one to the last digit of his own 1042.
This is the only check. The question "is this invoice Kevin's?" is never asked.

messages.label: 200 OK with the full invoice
messages.tip: To the server this is a normal, successful request, so no error is even logged.
A tiny script can download every invoice of every company within minutes.

aside.title: The number one risk on the list
aside.body: Broken Access Control is number one on OWASP's Top 10 web risks, and BOLA is number one on its API risks. Both are exactly this mistake. The reason is simple: exploiting it takes no hacking tools, only the curiosity to change a number in a URL.

items.meaning: Insecure Direct Object Reference: changing an id to get at someone else's data.
Broken Object Level Authorization: the name IDOR goes by in the API world.

check.q: How did Kevin read another company's invoice without cracking any password?
check.a: The app only checked that he was logged in. It never asked whether the invoice was his, so changing the id was enough to fetch any invoice.

slides.title: Two different questions: who are you, and is this yours?
slides.tldr: Authentication (AuthN) checks who you are; authorization (AuthZ) decides whether you may do this action on this thing.

blocks.title: The counter at a courier office
blocks.body: To collect a parcel you first show your photo ID at the counter. That is **authentication**: are you really Ryan? Then the clerk checks the register to see whether the parcel you're asking for was addressed to Ryan. That is **authorization**. A genuine ID still doesn't entitle Ryan to Kevin's parcel. And this second check happens for every parcel, not once a day.

blocks.caption: The two questions side by side, at the courier office and in your API

cells: May you do this to this thing?
rows.tip: The first answer is a person (or a service). The second is yes or no, and it depends on which thing and which action.

cells: Showing the ID at the counter
Matching the parcel to your name
rows.tip: The ID check happens once. But if you ask for ten parcels, the name is matched ten times.

cells: Once, at the start of the request
On every action, for every thing
rows.tip: The identity is worked out once and reused for the whole request. Permission is checked every time a thing is touched.
Proof of identity comes from the user. The permission rules live in your server code and data; the user never sends them.
401 means "identify yourself first". 403 means "I know who you are, but this is not for you", and logging in again won't help.

blocks.body: Authentication says who you are. Authorization says what you can do. Passing one does not pass the other.

aside.body: The N in AuthN is for name: who you are. The Z in AuthZ is for zone: which areas you may enter.

items: When a user asks for someone else's thing, many APIs return 404 instead of 403, so even its existence isn't revealed. Pick one and use it everywhere.
Authorization is meaningless without authentication: until you know who is asking, you can't decide what they may do.

items.label: Which error gets which status code

check.q: A logged-in user tries to cancel someone else's order. Which status code should the server return, and why not 401?
check.a: 403 Forbidden (or 404 to hide that the order exists). 401 means "identify yourself"; here the identity is known, the user just has no permission for this action on this thing.

slides.title: Where everything lives in Symfony Security
slides.tldr: The firewall's authenticator does AuthN. access_control, #[IsGranted] and voters do AuthZ, from coarse to fine in three layers.

blocks.body: Symfony has separate machinery for the two questions. The **firewall**'s authenticator reads the request's session cookie or token and works out who the user is. Permission is then checked in three layers: `access_control` guards a whole URL area, `#[IsGranted]` guards one action, and a **voter** checks ownership of one specific thing.

blocks.caption: The guards a request passes before it reaches the controller

nodes.label: Request
nodes.tip: A request from a browser or mobile app. The proof of identity travels in a cookie or the Authorization header.

nodes.label: Firewall
nodes.tip: The ID check at the courier counter. It reads the proof and finds the user; that identity is then used for the whole request.

nodes.label: access_control
nodes.tip: Coarse rules: which role is needed to enter this path. It knows nothing about any particular invoice or order.

nodes.label: #[IsGranted]
nodes.tip: A guard placed on one controller action. It can check roles, and it can also ask a voter.

nodes.label: Voter
nodes.tip: The finest layer: "does this invoice belong to this user?" Only this layer stops IDOR.
Returned when someone with no identity reaches a protected area, or when the cookie or token is no longer valid. The user must log in again.
The identity is known, but the role or ownership doesn't match. Logging in again won't change this answer.

edges.label: The request arrives, carrying a session cookie or token
No proof, or invalid proof: answer 401
Identity found: the user is now Ryan
URL rule passed: a login is enough here
The action asks: may Ryan see this invoice?
If the invoice isn't Ryan's, answer 403
Only if he owns it does the action run: 200

security:
    firewalls:
        main:
            lazy: true
            provider: app_user_provider
            json_login:                  # AuthN: checks email and password
                check_path: api_login
            logout:
                path: api_logout

    access_control:                      # AuthZ: coarse, by URL
        - { path: ^/api/login, roles: PUBLIC_ACCESS }
        - { path: ^/api/admin, roles: ROLE_ADMIN }
        - { path: ^/,          roles: IS_AUTHENTICATED_FULLY }

marks.tip: This is an authenticator. After a successful login Symfony stores the identity in the session and recognizes later requests by their cookie.
Only the first rule that matches from the top applies. So specific paths go first and general ones last.
The catch-all. A URL that matches no rule is open to everyone, so this last rule is what makes the default closed: a new route can't be entered without a login.

blocks.body: The default answer is "no". Permission must be granted separately, on purpose.

items: Symfony's access_control is open by default: a URL that matches no rule is allowed. End the list with a catch-all, and list public pages (login, health check) above it.
The price of a closed default: forget to list a public page and it answers 401. You notice at once, which is the safe way to fail.

check.q: `access_control` requires a login on the `^/api` path. Why do you still need a voter to stop IDOR?
check.a: `access_control` only looks at the URL and the role; it doesn't know whose invoice `/api/invoices/1043` is. Only a voter, or a query that filters by owner, can check ownership of a specific thing.

slides.title: Checking ownership on every object: the voter
slides.tldr: Write the ownership rule in one voter and call it with #[IsGranted] on each action. For lists, filter by owner in the query itself.

blocks.body: Put the courier clerk's question, "is this parcel in this person's name?", in one place: a **voter**. Every action that touches an invoice then calls that same rule through `#[IsGranted]`. When the rule changes, you change one file, not forty controllers. With it in place, Kevin's request for invoice 1043 ends in a 403 before the action even runs.

marks.tip: This voter only responds to the INVOICE_VIEW question on an Invoice object. For everything else it abstains.
No login means a straight "no". A voter's default answer should always be no.
The real rule is this one line: the invoice's company must be the same as the user's company.
Naming the argument in subject sends the $invoice below to the voter. If permission is denied, the response is 403 before the action even runs.
#[CurrentUser] provides the authenticated user from the session or token, never from a request parameter.
The filtering by company happens in the database, so other companies' rows never even reach PHP.

blocks.body: Wherever an id comes from (URL, body or query string), check ownership before you use it.

items: If you build the object by hand, call `$this->denyAccessUnlessGranted(InvoiceVoter::VIEW, $invoice)` inside the action. It does the same job.
Use separate attributes for writes: INVOICE_EDIT, INVOICE_DELETE. Being able to view something doesn't mean being able to change it.
Write a small unit test for the voter: owner gives yes, another company gives no, no login gives no.

items.label: Organizing rules by role, attribute and relationship
Filtering by company across the whole app

check.q: Why does the invoice detail action use a voter while the list action does not?
check.a: Fetching thousands of rows and running a voter on each is slow, and it breaks pagination. So the query itself filters by the logged-in user's company and returns only their rows.

slides.title: Four familiar gaps where other people's data leaks
slides.tldr: Taking userId from the request, hiding buttons in the UI, treating a UUID as a lock, and checking only GET: all four are broken authorization.

blocks.body: IDOR doesn't always show up as a number in the URL. The four mistakes below look different, but the disease is the same: the server trusted the client instead of checking for itself.

marks.tip: Change ?userId=7 to ?userId=8 and you get someone else's orders. Never take identity from a request parameter.
The client can no longer say "I am user 8". The server knows for itself who is logged in.

blocks.caption: Four gaps, why they break, and the right fix

cells: Use the user from the session or token
rows.tip: If userId, companyId or role comes from the body, query or a header, the client sets its own permissions.

cells: Hiding the button only in the UI
The API can be called directly
Check on the server, on every action
rows.tip: Hiding a "Delete" button with v-if in Vue only hides it from view. Anyone can call the endpoint with curl or DevTools, so the server is the last line of defense.

cells: Keep the UUID, but still check ownership
rows.tip: A UUID is hard to guess, but it isn't secret. Knowing an id is not the same as having permission.
It is very common to put a voter on the read action and forget the update or delete action. Attackers try every method.

blocks.body: What the client sends is a request, not proof. The server works out who is asking and what they may do.

items: The admin menu is hidden, but the `/api/admin/*` routes have no role check. This is called broken function-level authorization.
Accepting `roles` or `isAdmin` in a profile-update body (mass assignment). Keep only the allowed fields in the DTO.
Forgetting the check on file download, export and report endpoints. They hand out data too.

aside.body: Three questions for every endpoint: who is asking? which thing? which action?

items.label: Decisions on the server, the client only displays

check.q: The invoice id is now a UUID, nearly impossible to guess. Why can't you skip the ownership check?
check.a: A UUID is hard to guess but not secret: it leaks through links, emails, logs and screenshots. Without the check, whoever gets hold of an id gets the data.

slides.title: The read is guarded, the delete is not
slides.tldr: Guard every method of an endpoint, not just GET. A hidden button only hides the way in; the DELETE route is still open to anyone with curl.

blocks.body: After the fix, Kevin can no longer read invoice 1043. So he tries a different door: `DELETE /api/invoices/1043`. The delete button isn't in his screen, but curl doesn't need a button. The team had put a voter on the read action and forgotten the other one.

marks.tip: The same URL, a different method, a different guard. The role check says "logged in" and nothing about whose invoice this is.
Kevin deletes another company's invoice, and the server answers 204 like any normal success.
Its own attribute, INVOICE_DELETE. Add it to the voter's supports() with a stricter rule than viewing, such as same company and a billing role.

blocks.body: Every method of every endpoint needs its own check.

items: List your routes with `php bin/console debug:router` and check that each one with a write method has an #[IsGranted] or a denyAccessUnlessGranted() call.
Test the other methods too: log in as company A and try PATCH and DELETE on company B's invoice. Expect 403.
A Vue `v-if="user.isAdmin"` on the Delete button is design, not security. The server must refuse the request itself.

check.q: The Delete button is hidden for ordinary users in Vue. Why can Kevin still delete another company's invoice?
check.a: Hiding a button only hides the way in. He can send DELETE directly with curl, and the endpoint checked only that he was logged in, not whose invoice it was.

slides.title: Fired, but the token still works
slides.tldr: Once a self-contained JWT is issued, the server can't take it back before it expires. That is the revocation problem.

blocks.body: Logging in to the admin panel of Ryan's company gives you a 30-day JWT. Today employee Sarah is let go, and the admin sets her account to `disabled`. But the token in Sarah's browser says "Sarah, valid for 30 days", and the server only checks its signature without asking the database. So Sarah could keep getting in for another 29 days.

actors.tip: The dismissed employee. Her browser still holds a 30-day JWT.

actors.label: API
actors.tip: It only checks the JWT's signature and exp date; it never looks the user up in the database.

actors.label: Database
actors.tip: Here Sarah's account is disabled. But the API never asks for this information.

messages.tip: The token still has 29 days left.
The whole check is just math: does the signature match? The database is never touched.

messages.label: 200 OK with company reports
messages.tip: The dismissed employee is still receiving confidential reports.

aside.body: When a token is self-contained, the server doesn't have to remember anything, which makes scaling easy. But that is also the price: there is no way to take a token back.

items.meaning: JSON Web Token: a self-contained token that packs the user's details and a signature together.
Making an already-issued token useless before its expiry.

check.q: Why did Sarah's JWT keep working after her account was disabled?
check.a: The API only checked the signature and expiry, never the account status in the database. The token proves itself, so the server can't take it back before it expires.

slides.title: A name on a guest list, or a printed ticket?
slides.tldr: A session keeps state on the server (easy to revoke). A JWT carries state in the token (stateless, but hard to revoke).

blocks.title: The train ticket
blocks.body: A **session** is the guest list at the door: you only hold a slip with a number on it (the session id), and the real details sit on the list. When the manager strikes your name out, the slip is dead. A **JWT** is a printed ticket: the date and seat are written on it, and the train conductor just checks the stamp without opening any list. So it works with no list, but once a ticket is handed out, you can't pull it back.

blocks.caption: Session versus JWT: what you get, and what you give up

columns.title: Server-side session
items: Dead the moment you log out or ban
One store lookup on every request
Needs a shared store across many servers
Simplest and safest for browsers
columns.tip: State lives on the server (in Redis or the database). The client holds only a random id.

columns.title: JWT (self-contained)
items: Verified with no lookup
Works easily across many servers and services
Hard to cancel before it expires
Payload is encoded, not encrypted: anyone can read it
columns.tip: The user's details and a signature live in the token itself. The server only verifies the signature and remembers nothing.

blocks.body: A JWT payload is only base64-encoded, not secret. Never put passwords or confidential data in it.

use: A session, for your own browser-based app
Short-lived tokens for several services or a mobile API
avoid: Long-lived JWTs you have no way to revoke

items: Symfony's default firewall runs a session: you get cookie-based sessions without doing anything.
"JWT is modern, sessions are old" is a myth. Each is right in the right place.

check.q: For an app that serves only a browser frontend, session or JWT, and why?
check.a: A session. It is easy to revoke, the browser handles the cookie itself, and the stateless benefit of a JWT isn't needed here.

slides.title: Short-lived access tokens and refresh tokens
slides.tldr: The access token is a signed JWT that lasts 15 minutes. The refresh token lasts long, is single-use and stored hashed in the database, so a theft does limited damage.

blocks.body: The fix is two tokens. The **access token** is a signed JWT that lives 15 minutes: the API checks its signature and expiry, with no database lookup, so it stays fast. The **refresh token** lives 30 days, is a random string kept hashed in the database, and is used only to get a new access token. Each refresh spends the old one and issues a new pair (rotation). To lock Sarah out, delete her refresh tokens: her access token dies on its own and she can't get another.

blocks.caption: When the access token goes stale, the refresh token gets a fresh pair

nodes.tip: Verifies the JWT's signature and expiry on every request. No database call for the token itself.

nodes.tip: Holds each refresh token's SHA-256 hash, expiry and used flag. The real token is not stored.

After 15 minutes: 401, the access token is dead

            pattern: ^/api
            stateless: true
            access_token:

                        algorithms: ['HS256']
                        keyset: '%env(JWT_KEYSET)%'
                        audience: 'company-api'
                        issuers: ['company-api']

The oidc handler verifies a signed JWT: signature, expiry, audience and issuer. It reads no token table.
The signing key comes from an environment secret, never from git.
Look the token up by its hash. A missing row means revoked or never issued.
Reuse detection: a token that was already spent is back, so cut off the whole family.
Rotation: the old token is marked used, and a brand-new one is issued.

items.meaning: A random string that means nothing by itself. Only the server's database knows whose it is.
Swapping the refresh token for a new one on every use, so each one works once.

items: Make refresh tokens opaque random strings from random_bytes(32), and never pack any data into them.
The admin's "disable user" action should call revokeAllFor() too, or the ban only takes effect when the refresh token expires.

items.label: Revoking every session when the password changes
Keeping the signing key out of git

check.q: Why is the refresh token stored hashed in the database, and what does rotation give you?
check.a: If the database leaks, the hash doesn't reveal the real token. With rotation every refresh issues a new token, so a spent one showing up again exposes a theft.

slides.title: What a ban costs: up to 15 minutes
slides.tldr: With short tokens a ban bites within 15 minutes, not 29 days. If that is too slow, you pay with a lookup on every request.

blocks.body: Ryan's admin disables Sarah at 10:00. Her access token was issued at 09:55, so it runs until 10:10. Until then the API still accepts it. At 10:10 it expires, and her refresh attempt finds no row in the database. The worst case is 15 minutes instead of 29 days. That wait is the price of never asking the database about each request.

check.a: Check the user (or a denylist of banned ids) on every request, or use a server session. You pay one read per request for an instant ban.

slides.title: Where to keep the token: not localStorage
slides.tldr: Any XSS can read a token in localStorage. An HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite cookie is out of JavaScript's reach.

blocks.body: Many people keep the token in `localStorage` because it's easy. The problem is that one XSS hole on the page lets an attacker's script read that token and send it to their own server. JavaScript can't read an `HttpOnly` cookie; the browser just attaches it to requests by itself.

marks.tip: Every value in localStorage is readable by any JavaScript on the page, including third-party scripts.
HttpOnly: even with XSS, a script can't see this cookie's value.
SameSite=Strict keeps the cookie off requests that come from other sites, a shield against CSRF.
Limiting the path means the cookie goes only to the refresh route, not with other requests.

blocks.body: Never put a token in localStorage. The refresh token belongs in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie.

items: Keeping the access token in a cookie brings CSRF risk, so set SameSite and think about CSRF tokens on state-changing requests.
The access token can live in Vue's memory (Pinia state). After a page reload, fetch a new one using the refresh cookie.

check.q: An HttpOnly cookie doesn't make XSS harmless. So why is it still better to keep the refresh token there?
check.a: A script can still send requests, but it can't steal the token to a server of its own and use it from elsewhere indefinitely. The damage is limited to the time the user is on that page.

slides.title: A new app asks for your Gmail password
slides.tldr: Handing your password to another app hands over all your power. OAuth2 gives limited, expiring, revocable permission instead.

blocks.body: A photo-printing app says, "To fetch your pictures from Google Photos, give us your Gmail email and password." If you do, the app can read more than photos: your email, your Drive, everything. And unless you change your password, it can keep that access forever. If the app's database ever leaks, your Google account goes with it. What we want is "photos only, for today only, and I can shut it off any time."

blocks.caption: Giving a password versus an OAuth2 grant

columns.title: Giving the app your password
items: Full power, no limits
No expiry: it lasts forever
To cut it off you must change the password
If the app leaks, your Google account leaks
columns.tip: The app can then do anything as you. There is no way to block individual actions.

columns.title: An OAuth2 grant
items: Only the actions named in the scope (such as reading photos)
Access tokens are short-lived
Revoke it in one click from Google's settings
If the app leaks, only that scope is at risk
columns.tip: The app never sees your password. It receives a limited token with an expiry.

aside.title: A lesson from the early social web
aside.body: Years ago, many sites said "enter your email password so we can find your friends." OAuth came along to end exactly that habit: the password stays with the one who owns it, and everyone else gets a separate key.

check.q: What do you gain by giving an app an OAuth2 token instead of your password?
check.a: The app can do only what the scope allows, the token expires, and you can revoke it from Google at any time. The password never reaches the app.

slides.title: Who is involved, and what OAuth2, OIDC and SAML are each for
slides.tldr: OAuth2 grants permission (authorization). OIDC adds "who is this" on top. SAML does the same job in an older XML style, for corporate SSO.

blocks.title: The building guard and the visitor slip
blocks.body: Ryan (the **resource owner**) tells the building guard (the **authorization server**), "This courier (the **client**) may open my mailbox, and nothing else." The guard hands over a slip (the **access token**) saying mailbox only (the **scope**) and valid until 5 pm today. The mailbox (the **resource server**) opens when it sees the slip. If the guard also hands over an ID card saying "this is Ryan from apartment 302", that is **OIDC's id_token**.

blocks.caption: The three protocols at a glance

rows.tip: OAuth2 only says "this is allowed". OIDC adds "this person is so-and-so". SAML says the same thing in XML.
Treating OAuth2 alone as proof of login is a mistake: an access token doesn't say who it was issued for.
OIDC's id_token is always a JWT. A SAML assertion is a much bigger XML document.
Older enterprise software at big companies still asks for SAML. New projects usually go with OIDC.

blocks.body: OAuth2 is for permission, not for login. To learn who someone is, you need OIDC's id_token.

items.meaning: The list of actions a token may perform, such as photos.read.
Identity Provider: the party that verifies identity (Google, Okta).
Single sign-on: log in once and get into many apps.

aside.body: OAuth2 = what you can do. OIDC = who you are. SAML = OIDC's older, XML-flavored cousin.

check.q: Does holding an OAuth2 access token tell you who the person is? If not, what do you need?
check.a: No. An access token expresses permission, not identity. To learn identity you take OIDC's id_token and verify its iss, aud, exp and nonce.

slides.title: Authorization code + PKCE, step by step
slides.tldr: Only a single-use code travels through the browser. The server swaps it for tokens, and PKCE's code_verifier proves that the same party started the flow.

blocks.body: Today the only acceptable approach is the **authorization code flow**. The browser makes the round trip carrying just a short code, and the real tokens arrive over direct server-to-server contact. **PKCE** is an extra lock: at the start the app creates a secret `code_verifier` and sends its hash (the `code_challenge`); at the end it shows the original verifier to prove the code wasn't snatched by someone else.

actors.tip: Ryan's browser. It only carries redirects; the real tokens never pass through it.

actors.label: Our app

actors.tip: The authorization server. It logs Ryan in, asks for consent, and issues the code and tokens.

Only Google sees the password, never our app.

messages.label: id_token + access_token
messages.tip: The app now verifies the id_token claims, recognizes Ryan and logs him in.

marks.tip: The verifier is 32 random secret bytes. The challenge is only its hash, so even if it is stolen the verifier stays hidden.
state blocks CSRF: if the returned state doesn't match the session, we never started this request.
nonce ties the id_token to this particular login attempt, so an old token can't be replayed.
With openid in the scope, this is an OIDC login, not just OAuth2.

items: Clients that can't keep a secret (a Vue SPA, a mobile app), called public clients, must use PKCE. These days even confidential clients should use it too.
Don't build the authorize URL by hand. Use a well-maintained library such as `league/oauth2-client` or `knpuniversity/oauth2-client-bundle`.

check.q: Even if an attacker steals the code from the redirect, why can't they get tokens when PKCE is used?
check.a: Requesting tokens needs the original `code_verifier`, which exists only in the session of the app that started the flow. The thief knows just the code and the hash (challenge), and a verifier can't be recovered from its hash.

slides.title: The user is back: trust nothing you haven't verified
slides.tldr: In the callback, check state, exchange the code, then check the id_token's iss, aud, exp and nonce. For API access tokens, use Symfony's oidc handler.

blocks.body: You can't accept the guard's ID card without looking at it either: who issued it (`iss`), who it's for (`aud` = our client_id), when it expires (`exp`), and whether it belongs to this very login (`nonce`). In the code below the id_token arrived straight from Google's token endpoint over TLS, so under the OIDC spec checking these claims is enough in place of the signature. If it had come through the browser, you would have to verify the signature too.

marks.tip: If the state doesn't match, stop here. remove() means it is deleted from the session after one use.
The second part (the payload) is base64url-encoded JSON. The signature check is skipped here because the token came straight from Google over HTTPS.
Four checks: who issued it, who it's for, whether it has expired, and whether the nonce belongs to this login.
An email can change; the stable key for recognizing a user is the sub claim.

blocks.code:
security:
    firewalls:
        api:
            pattern: ^/api
            stateless: true
            access_token:
                token_handler:
                    oidc:
                        algorithms: ['ES256']
                        issuers: ['https://accounts.example.com']
                        audience: 'orders-api'
                        keyset: '%env(OIDC_JWKS)%'

marks.tip: If our own API accepts JWT access tokens from another IdP, Symfony's built-in oidc handler verifies the signature.
Checking the audience means a token issued for another API won't work here.

items.desc: How the access_token handler is set up on the api firewall
Every option of the oidc handler

check.q: What is the risk of not checking `aud` in an id_token?
check.a: Someone could bring a valid token from the same IdP that was issued for a different app and log in to ours. The signature would be genuine, but the token was never meant for us.

slides.title: Familiar mistakes in OAuth
slides.tldr: Skipping state, wildcards in redirect_uri, the implicit flow, treating an access token as login, and a client secret in an SPA: all five break OAuth.

blocks.body: OAuth itself is solid, but mistakes in using it open holes. The five below are the ones you see most. Behind each lies the same cause: assuming something that should have been verified.

blocks.caption: Five mistakes, what happens, and the right way

cells: An attacker's code lands in your session
A random state every time; match it on return
rows.tip: An attacker can send the code from their own account to a victim and attach their Google account to the victim's account.

cells: The code or token goes to an attacker's URL
Register the full URL exactly at the IdP
rows.tip: With https://app.com/* allowed, a single open redirect is enough to steal a code.

cells: The token drifts around the browser in the URL
rows.tip: The implicit flow is nearly deprecated: the token leaks into history, logs and the referrer.

cells: A token for another app gets you in
Take the id_token and check iss/aud/nonce
rows.tip: An access token is for APIs; the app can't tell who it was issued for.

cells: Anyone can find it in DevTools
Public client: PKCE without a secret
rows.tip: Whatever sits in the browser or inside a mobile app isn't secret. A secret belongs only on the server.

blocks.body: Match the redirect URI exactly, check state and nonce every time, and use only code + PKCE.

items: Matching accounts by email: linking an account even though the IdP didn't say the email was verified (email_verified) is a path to account takeover.
Using the email instead of the id_token's `sub` as the key; if the email changes, someone else's account may open up.

items.label: A way to think about what can go wrong in a feature

check.q: Why is a wildcard like `https://app.com/*` in redirect_uri dangerous?
check.a: Through any open redirect in the app, the code (or token) can be sent to an attacker's URL. That is why you register the full URL exactly at the IdP.

slides.title: From ROLE_MANAGER to 40 roles
slides.tldr: Starting with roles alone is easy. But once conditions like "own department, expenses under $500" arrive, the number of roles explodes.

blocks.body: Ryan's expense-approval app starts with two roles: `ROLE_EMPLOYEE` and `ROLE_MANAGER`. Then the rules arrive. A manager may approve only expenses from their own department. Anything above $500 needs a director. Nobody may approve their own expense. For each new condition Ryan creates another role. Six months later there are 40 roles and nobody can say which one is for whom.

blocks.caption: What you end up with when every condition becomes its own role

steps.title: 1. Two roles
steps.body: ROLE_EMPLOYEE, ROLE_MANAGER
steps.tip: A simple, clean start. For a small app this is enough.

steps.title: 2. By department
steps.body: ROLE_MANAGER_SALES, ROLE_MANAGER_HR...
steps.tip: A separate role for every department. Add a department and you add a role.

steps.title: 3. By limit
steps.body: ROLE_MANAGER_SALES_UPTO_500
steps.tip: The money limit has crept into the role too. Now it is department × limit, and the count multiplies.

steps.title: 4. 40 roles
steps.body: Nobody can remember them all
steps.tip: For example 8 departments times 5 variants each is already 40. When a new hire joins, working out which roles to assign becomes a small research project.

steps.title: 5. The way out
steps.body: Three roles, and one voter that checks the facts
steps.tip: Department and limit are facts about the expense, so one rule checks them against the expense. No new role per department.

aside.body: A role answers "who are you?". But permission really depends on "which thing, in what state, for how much". Cram that into roles and they explode.

items.meaning: The number of roles blowing up because conditions multiply.
Role-based access control: permission decided by the user's role, their title, alone.

check.q: Why is "a manager approves only their own department's expenses" a problem when written as one role per department?
check.a: Departments and limits multiply the number of roles, and every new department means changing code and data. The department isn't a role; it is a fact about the thing, so check it against the thing.

slides.title: Titles, conditions and relationships: three kinds of rules
slides.tldr: RBAC looks at titles, ABAC at facts about the user, the thing and the environment, ReBAC at the relationship to the thing. When rules get complex, use a policy engine.

blocks.title: The bank vault room
blocks.body: Picture three rules for entering a vault. **RBAC**: "managers may enter", the title alone. **ABAC**: "a manager, in their own branch's vault, during office hours, for transactions under 5 million", a title plus conditions. **ReBAC**: "whoever is a joint owner of this locker may open it", where the relationship to the locker is the permission. And a **policy engine** is writing every rule in one rulebook and asking an outside judge for the verdict.

blocks.caption: The approaches side by side

cells: The relationship of user and thing
rows.tip: RBAC is the simplest. In ABAC any fact (department, amount, time) can enter a rule. In ReBAC rules look like a graph: who is connected to what.

cells: Editor of the folder, so also of the file
rows.tip: Google Drive sharing is exactly ReBAC: be an editor of a folder and you are an editor of the files inside.

cells: A small app with a few titles
rows.tip: Most apps start with RBAC and move on to ABAC. ReBAC is for sharing-heavy systems.

cells: Looking up relationships in a voter
rows.tip: All three run on Symfony's same voter system. You can apply them without any policy engine.

blocks.body: A role says which team you're on. Permission is decided by facts about the thing and your relationship to it.

use: RBAC: a simple app based on titles
A policy engine: the same rules across many services, or when you want to change rules without deploying code
avoid: A policy engine: one Symfony monolith with a few rules, where voters are enough

items.meaning: Attribute-based: facts about the user, the thing and the time. Relationship-based: how the user is connected to the thing.
Policy engines that take rules written outside your code and return the decision.
Google's ReBAC system and its open-source counterpart.

check.q: "If you are an editor of the folder a file is in, you can change the file too." Which model is this?
check.a: ReBAC. The permission comes from the user's relationship to the folder, and it is inherited by the files inside.

slides.title: Role + conditions: writing an ABAC voter
slides.tldr: A role hierarchy gives the coarse permission, a voter checks facts about the thing (department, amount, owner) for the fine rules, and #[IsGranted] guards the action.

blocks.body: Instead of 40 roles, keep three (employee, manager, director) and move the rules into one voter. Each role includes the one below it: `role_hierarchy: {ROLE_MANAGER: ROLE_EMPLOYEE, ROLE_DIRECTOR: ROLE_MANAGER}` in `security.yaml`. The voter checks department, amount and "not their own expense". A manager's limit is $500; a director has none.

marks.tip: No login or no role means "no" right here. When in doubt, always false.
ROLE_DIRECTOR sits above ROLE_MANAGER, so a director passes the check above and has no limit. A $700 expense: manager no, director yes.
The department lives in the Expense, not in a role. A new department needs no code change.
Separation of duties: the person who made the request can't approve it themselves.
The rule lives in one place. Whether approval comes from the web, the API or a console command, the same voter runs.

items.desc: Every registered voter
How the role hierarchy is laid out

items.meaning: A small class Symfony asks: "may this user do this to that thing?" It answers yes or no.

items: Unit-test the voter: right-department manager yes; other department no; own expense no; $700 manager no, director yes.

check.q: Why does the manager's "own department" condition belong in the voter and not in a role?
check.a: Department is a fact about the user and the thing, not a title. In a voter, a new department needs no code change and adds no roles.

slides.title: Permission by relationship: from folder to file
slides.tldr: In ReBAC the voter climbs up from the thing (file → folder → project) looking for any grant to the user. The relation it finds is the permission.

blocks.body: In a file-sharing app the rule is: whoever is an `editor` of a folder is an `editor` of every file inside. Rather than keeping a grant on each file, the voter climbs from the file up through its folders, and the first grant it finds is the user's relationship. The grants live in an ordinary database table.

check.q: What do you gain by using folder grants instead of keeping a separate grant on every file?
check.a: Make someone an editor of the folder once and it applies automatically to every file inside, including new ones. Changing permission means changing a single row.

slides.title: Four slippery spots in authorization
slides.tldr: Scattered ifs, defaulting to "yes", stale roles frozen into a token, and guarding only some actions: each one breaks the rules in a different way.

marks.tip: A strict array comparison and a hardcoded email are both brittle. A director has roles [DIRECTOR, MANAGER, EMPLOYEE], so this check wrongly refuses the director.
If the condition matches it approves; otherwise it silently returns an empty JSON. Without permission it should return 403.

blocks.caption: Four slippery spots: what breaks, and the right way

cells: ifs and role names scattered everywhere
The rule changes in 39 of 40 places; one hole stays open
The rule in one voter, called with #[IsGranted]
rows.tip: To change the rule you have to hunt through forty places, and missing one leaves a hole. With one voter, you change one place.

cells: A new EXPORT action ships and everyone can export
The default is always false (deny by default)
rows.tip: For an attribute it doesn't recognize or a state it doesn't know, the voter returns `false`. The next slide shows it in code.

cells: Packing roles into the token at login
Read the current roles from the database on each request
rows.tip: The token was signed at 09:30 and still says "manager" until it expires. The price of the fix is one user read per request, which Symfony's user provider already does.

cells: An employee sends DELETE and it goes through
Guard every action, export and download too
rows.tip: Putting a voter on the view action and forgetting the delete action is a very familiar mistake. The next slide shows it.

blocks.body: Write the permission rule in one place, keep the default at "no", and call it on every action.

aside.title: The stale manager
aside.body: Sarah is demoted at 10:00. The token she logged in with at 09:30 lives for one hour and still carries ROLE_MANAGER. At 10:20 she approves a $400 expense, because the API trusts the token. Loading her roles from the database on each request would have refused her at 10:00.

items: Symfony's `access_decision_manager` strategy defaults to `affirmative`: one voter saying yes is enough. If you want any objecting voter to block access, use `unanimous`.
Keep an audit log of who got which permission and when. You will need to trace permission changes later.

check.q: An employee was promoted, but their old access token still carries the previous role. Which design avoids the problem?
check.a: Load the user's current roles from the database on every request (for example with an opaque token), or keep the token lifetime very short so a stale role doesn't last long.

slides.title: Deny by default, guard every action
slides.tldr: A voter that ends in "return true" lets every new action through. End it in false, and put a guard on every route, export and delete included.

blocks.body: A month after launch, someone adds an `EXPENSE_EXPORT` action to the controller and forgets to teach the voter about it. The voter's last line is `return true`, so the new action is allowed for everybody, and any employee can download the whole company's expenses. The fix is a voter that ends in `false`, and a guard on every action.

marks.tip: supports() accepts every attribute, so this voter now answers for actions it was never written for.
Anything that is not APPROVE falls through to yes. The hole opens the day a new action appears.
Only known attributes are claimed. If no voter claims one, Symfony denies it, because allow_if_all_abstain is false by default.
The last word is no. A new action stays closed until someone writes its rule on purpose.

blocks.caption: The second half of the fix: a guard on every route, not only the view

columns.title: Guard on view only
items: GET /expenses/7: the voter runs
DELETE /expenses/7: no guard, any employee deletes
GET /expenses/export.csv: no guard, everyone downloads
columns.tip: The developer protected the page everyone looks at and forgot the others.

columns.title: Guard on every action
items: #[IsGranted] on show, approve, delete and export
A test calls every route as a plain employee and expects 403
columns.tip: Each route names its own permission, so a forgotten one is easy to spot in review.

items: List every route with `php bin/console debug:router` and check that each one has `#[IsGranted]` or an `access_control` line.
Write one test per sensitive action: a plain employee gets 403. It is the cheapest way to catch a forgotten guard.

check.q: Someone adds an EXPORT action but forgets the voter. Who can export if the voter ends in `return true`, and who if it ends in `default => false`?
check.a: With `return true`, everyone can. With `default => false`, nobody can until a rule for EXPORT is written on purpose.

slides.title: One forgotten WHERE, and every company's data in one place
slides.tldr: When many customers (tenants) share one database, every query must filter by tenant. Forget it in one query and one customer sees another's data.

blocks.body: Ryan's HR software (SaaS) keeps employee data for 300 companies in one database. Every query has to carry `WHERE tenant_id = ?`, and Ryan's team followed that rule. One day a new developer wrote the query for an export report and left the condition out. The HR manager of company A downloaded the Excel file and found the salary list of all 300 companies in it.

marks.tip: The new developer didn't remember. Code review struggles to catch this too, because nothing bad was written; something was just left out.

blocks.caption: With the condition missing, rows of every tenant come back together

nodes.label: Company A HR
nodes.tip: The logged-in user, who should see only their own company's employees.

nodes.label: API
nodes.tip: This query has no tenant filter.

nodes.label: employee table
nodes.tip: Every customer's data sits in one table, told apart only by the tenant_id column.

edges.label: Asks for an export
Asks for all employees, with no tenant

aside.body: If you rely on writing the condition by hand in every query, someone will eventually forget. Security can't depend on human memory.

items.meaning: One customer of the system (a company) whose data must stay separate from everyone else's.
Software as a service: offering the same software to many customers.

check.q: The rule was to write the `tenant_id` condition by hand in every query. Why did data leak anyway?
check.a: One query lacked the condition. Relying on memory makes a mistake inevitable, so the filter has to sit somewhere it is applied to every query automatically.

slides.title: A bunk in a shared room, an apartment, or a separate house
slides.tldr: Three levels of tenant separation: a tenant_id in shared tables (row), a separate schema, a separate database. The more separate, the safer and the pricier.

blocks.title: Rental housing
blocks.body: **Row-level**: many tenants put their bunk beds in one big hostel room. It's cheap, but the risk of one person's things ending up in another's hands is highest. **Schema-level**: separate apartments in one building, each with its own door. **Database-level**: everyone gets their own house. And a **noisy neighbor** is the apartment next door that plays music all night or uses up all the water.

blocks.caption: The pros and cons of the three levels

rows.tip: The same tables, a separate set of tables, and a separate server connection: three degrees of separation.
With separate databases, even a wrong query can't touch anyone else's data. In row-level, the only barrier is the condition being right.
Running 5,000 databases for 5,000 tenants, with a migration on each, is a huge operational burden.

cells: Biggest risk, everyone in one database
rows.tip: One tenant's heavy query can slow everyone's database. With separate databases that effect can be contained.
Most SaaS products start row-level. For big customers or legal requirements they give those customers their own database.

blocks.body: The higher the risk of mixing data, the further you move from the bunk toward the house, and the cost and security both go up.

use: Row-level: many small customers, a fast-growing SaaS
Database per tenant: a few large customers, strict isolation or data residency
avoid: Database per tenant: thousands of small tenants, where the operational burden is unbearable

check.q: A large bank says it won't sign unless its data is in a separate database. What do you do for the other 500 small customers?
check.a: A separate database for the bank, and row-level for the small ones. Mixing levels according to a customer's risk and value is the usual practice.

slides.title: A Doctrine filter: scoping every query by tenant automatically
slides.tldr: An SQLFilter adds `tenant_id = ?` to every Doctrine query for you. Enable it at the start of the request with the logged-in user's tenant.

blocks.body: Think of a building guard who says "only your own apartment" before anyone goes in. In Doctrine that guard is the **SQL filter**. It appends `AND tenant_id = ?` to every DQL query on its own, so developers don't have to remember. The story's `exportAll()`, with no WHERE written, now runs as `... WHERE e.tenant_id = '7' ORDER BY e.name`, so company A's file holds only company A. Entities that belong to a tenant implement a `TenantAware` interface; the next slide registers the filter and stamps new rows.

marks.tip: Doctrine calls this method for every entity; the condition it returns is added to the query's WHERE.
getParameter() quotes the value for you, so there is no SQL injection. Never splice user input into the string.
The firewall's listener has priority 8; we run after it, at 4, so the user is already identified.
The tenant comes from the logged-in user, never from the request's query or headers.

items.cmd: php bin/console debug:config doctrine orm filters
items.desc: Whether the filter is registered

items: The filter works only on ORM/DQL queries. Raw DBAL SQL and native queries don't get it, so they need the condition written by hand.
Don't disable this filter in the app's main code; turn it off only deliberately, for admin or cross-tenant work.
The price: every query now filters on tenant_id, so put it first in your indexes, such as (tenant_id, created_at), or large tables get slow.

check.q: Why is the tenant id taken from the logged-in user instead of a `?tenant=7` request parameter?
check.a: The parameter is in the client's hands; they could write someone else's tenant and see their data. The logged-in user's tenant is information the server has verified.

slides.title: Registering the filter and stamping new rows
slides.tldr: Register the filter in doctrine.yaml, and stamp the tenant on every new row in a prePersist listener. The filter guards reads; this guards writes.

blocks.body: A filter that isn't registered does nothing, and calling `enable('tenant')` on it throws an error. And the filter only trims what you read. A new row saved with no tenant would be invisible to everyone, because `tenant_id = 7` never matches NULL. So two more pieces are needed.

blocks.code:
doctrine:
    orm:
        filters:
            tenant:
                class: App\Doctrine\TenantFilter
                enabled: false       # the request listener turns it on

marks.tip: This name, tenant, is the one you pass to getFilters()->enable('tenant').
Off by default: the request listener enables it once the user is known. Console commands and workers must enable it themselves.
Runs just before any new entity is inserted.
The tenant is copied from the verified user, so a client can't save a row into another company. A worker has no user, so there you set the tenant yourself.

blocks.body: The filter trims what you read. Stamping the tenant guards what you write.

items: Add a database NOT NULL on tenant_id, so a row that slips through with no tenant fails loudly instead of vanishing.
When not to use this: if one customer's data must never share a database with others (a bank, a regulator's rule), use a database per tenant instead.

check.q: A new Employee is saved with no tenant set. Why does it vanish from every company's lists?
check.a: The filter adds `tenant_id = 7`, and a NULL tenant matches no number. The prePersist listener stamps the user's tenant on every new row so this never happens.

slides.title: Keeping one tenant from using up everyone's water
slides.tldr: A per-tenant rate limit, separate queues or worker shares, and limits on heavy jobs stop one customer's load from slowing the rest.

blocks.body: In row-level tenancy all tenants share one database and one set of servers. If one customer sends a million requests an hour (about 280 knocks on the door every second, all day), the other 299 slow down. So each tenant needs its own water meter: a **per-tenant rate limit**. In Symfony's RateLimiter, use the tenant's id as the key and every customer gets a separate bucket.

blocks.code:
framework:
    rate_limiter:
        tenant_api:
            policy: 'sliding_window'
            limit: 600
            interval: '1 minute'

marks.tip: The name is `tenant_api`, so Symfony autowires `RateLimiterFactory $tenantApiLimiter`.
Each tenant gets 600 requests a minute, 10 a second: plenty for a busy HR team, far below a runaway script. You can raise it for bigger plans.
With the tenant as the key, each tenant is counted separately. Keyed by user or IP, all employees of a big company would wrongly share one count.
It returns 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After time, so the client knows how long to wait before trying again.

items.desc: PostgreSQL: cancel a report query that runs longer than 5 seconds
A worker only for heavy reports, so they never block the emails

items: Route heavy report messages to their own transport (`reports`), so one tenant's flood of reports queues behind itself, not in front of everyone's email.
The limiter counts in a cache. With more than one app server, point it at a shared store such as Redis, or each server counts alone and the real limit is multiplied.

items.label: Kinds of rate limits and their algorithms

check.q: What changes when the rate-limit key is the tenant id instead of the user id?
check.a: The limit is counted in one bucket for the whole company, so a single company's employees together can't eat into another company's share. But within that company, the employees do have to share the limit.

slides.title: Four ways data seeps through even with a filter
slides.tldr: Raw SQL, background workers, cache keys and unique indexes: the Doctrine filter doesn't reach these four places, so tenant must be handled separately there.

blocks.body: The filter is a good barrier, but there are gaps around it where Doctrine's guard isn't standing. The fix is the same for each: carry the tenant along explicitly, rather than guessing.

blocks.caption: Four gaps, what happens, and the right way

cells: The filter doesn't run; all tenants come back
Write `tenant_id = :t` by hand, or use the ORM
rows.tip: When you run SQL directly instead of DQL, the Doctrine filter doesn't know about it. Complex report queries make this mistake most often.

cells: No request, so the filter is off
Put tenantId in the message, enable the filter in the handler
rows.tip: Background jobs have no logged-in user; without enabling the filter, they touch every row regardless of tenant.

cells: `report.2024` is the same for all tenants
Put the tenant in the key: `t7.report.2024`
rows.tip: A cache key without a tenant means showing company A's report to company B.

cells: Email must be unique across all tenants
rows.tip: Two companies can easily have an employee with the same email. A unique index without tenant means one of them can't register.

marks.tip: A worker runs all day and takes messages from many tenants; set the right tenant in every handler.
The :t placeholder is bound, never spliced into the string, so there is no SQL injection.
Cache keys carrying the tenant mean company A's cached report can never be served to company B.
On the Employee entity (or in a migration): the same email may exist once per tenant.

blocks.body: The filter is a barrier, not the last line of defense. In raw SQL, workers, caches and unique indexes, carry the tenant yourself.

items.cmd: ALTER TABLE employee ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
items.desc: From now on the table needs a policy before rows are visible

items.cmd: CREATE POLICY tenant_only ON employee USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::int);
items.desc: The database itself hides other tenants' rows, even when raw SQL forgets the WHERE

items: The price of RLS: the app must run `SET app.tenant_id = ...` on every connection it takes from the pool, and a mistake there blocks everything. Test it first.
Write a test for cross-tenant leaks: create two tenants, and asking for the other's data with one tenant's token must give 403/404.

check.q: Why isn't the Doctrine tenant filter enabled automatically in a Messenger worker, and what should you do?
check.a: The filter is enabled from the web request's logged-in user, and a worker has no request. So put the tenantId in the message and enable the filter with that id in the handler.

slides.title: Account takeover through a guessable reset link
slides.tldr: Forgot-password is a back door weaker than the front door. If the reset token is guessable, an attacker can open any account.

blocks.body: Login in Ryan's app is very solid: hashed passwords, and a limit on wrong attempts. But for the "I forgot my password" feature he built the reset-link token from the email with `md5`. The attacker knows Sarah's email, so on his own computer he built the same token, opened the reset link directly and changed Sarah's password. The front door was locked, but the back door was wide open.

marks.tip: md5 is a fingerprint function: the same email always gives the same result, and anyone can compute it. A reset token must be something only the server and the inbox owner know.

blocks.caption: The attacker built the token from the email himself and took Sarah's account
